Breaking: Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A Newly introduced Frontier and Use Cases

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2080 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads.
  • It has been revealed that every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory.
  • The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs.

It has been revealed that every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next.

The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome.

It has been revealed that IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action.

Industry observers note that foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to new series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic.

Figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them.

In a recent development, now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy (documentation). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.(documentation). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs.

The models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made.

See how time series and real-time context come together to create value:.

In a recent development, businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that revision at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening.

According to recent reports, A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state.

According to recent reports, figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere.

Time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate.

Recent findings suggest that figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them.

This approach can help teams in four ways:.

Sources indicate that -Scale model development. A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one.

-Refresh predictions as data changes. Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration.

-Put signals closer to decisions. Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment.

-Run compact models on CPUs. The models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, in the cloud or on premises, which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure and simplify deployment.

Figure 4. Stream native time-series intelligence on Confluent.

The following scenarios illustrate how organizations could combine time-series models, streaming data, and application logic.

It has been revealed that an ice cream line’s quality depends on overrun—the amount of air whipped into the mix. Today, the process engineer and operator rely on QA lab measurements taken after the tubs are filled. If a newly introduced cream lot or a warm, humid day changes the process, hours of production may already need rework by the time the team sees the result.

To get ahead of the problem, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes. It forecasts the share of tubs expected to be in spec four hours ahead, along with a likely range.

When the forecast falls below the plant’s target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow. Because the model takes these control variables as inputs, it can score each option before anything changes on the line. The operator approves the recommended setpoints, while routine adjustments can be automated within predefined guardrails.

The outcome is a more proactive process: less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality. The same approach can be applied to ovens, dryers, kilns, and mills.

Sources indicate that figure 5. A forecast of product quality helps the operator evaluate freezer setpoints before making an adjustment.

Recent findings suggest that A store operations team monitors sales for thousands of products across hundreds of stores. Fixed thresholds often flag predictable weekend peaks while missing quieter changes, such as a product selling less than expected. As alerts accumulate, it becomes harder for the team to know where to focus.

Industry observers note that AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on its recent history. Each upcoming reading is compared with that range at a confidence level the team chooses, without training a separate model for every product and store.

According to recent reports, when sales fall outside the expected range, the signal can be combined with inventory and store data to help identify a likely cause and recommend a next step—for example, checking the shelf or replenishing stock. The same approach can be applied to machine sensors, API telemetry, meter readings, and payment volumes.

Figure 6. Store sales are compared with an expected range. In the view shown, recurring peaks remain within the range and no anomaly is flagged.

A category planner and a replenishment team need to keep products available across every store without carrying excess inventory. But forecasts may be refreshed only once a week, often focusing on top-selling products, while the long tail is managed with simpler rules. When sales patterns change between planning cycles, one store can run out while another has too much stock.

With AI_FORECAST, a pretrained model can forecast demand across products and stores. In this example, it produces a 28-day forecast with a P10–P90 range, refreshed as upcoming sales data arrives. The planning application combines the forecast with inventory, lead time, and the planner’s chosen service level to calculate a reorder point.

Industry observers note that when stock is projected to fall below that point, an agent can draft a purchase order for review. The same approach can support planning for spare parts, staffing, ATM cash, and energy demand.

Industry observers note that figure 7. A store-level demand forecast informs a reorder point and a proposed purchase order for oat milk.

Sources indicate that fraud teams already rely on sophisticated rules and models to evaluate transactions. One continuing challenge is that a threshold applied across many cardholders may not reflect how each person normally spends.

According to recent reports, A time-series signal can add that individual context. In this example, each payment is compared with an expected spending range based on the card’s recent history. A transaction outside that range is passed to the bank’s existing fraud systems as an additional input, alongside other signals and business rules.

The bank can then decide whether to approve the payment, request additional authentication, or investigate further. The decision and the signals behind it can be retained for review.

Figure 8.A payment outside the card’s expected spending range prompts a step-up authentication in an illustrative fraud workflow.

It has been revealed that an execution desk needs to divide a large order into smaller trades while managing its effect on the market. Historical volume curves offer a starting point, but today’s trading activity may look very different from the average.

According to recent reports, on each one-minute bar, PatchTST-FM forecasts trading volume for the next 30 minutes, with a P10–P90 range. The execution algorithm uses that forecast to pace the order within the participation limit set by the desk.

If a news event changes market activity, the algorithm can pause and replan. If trading is quieter than expected, it can reduce the size of each slice and signal that the order may take longer to complete. Each forecast and the resulting execution decisions can be retained in the audit trail.

Figure 9. Volume forecast informs the proposed execution schedule for a 100,000-share order.

A reliability engineer investigating an unusual sensor pattern may want to know whether similar behavior appeared elsewhere in the plant.

TSPulse can produce representations of time-series windows that support similarity search. In a separately built application, those representations could be indexed and used to retrieve historical patterns across equipment. An engineer could search for shapes such as a spike and recovery, a gradual rise, or a step change, then inspect the associated maintenance records and operating conditions.

This application requires an embedding pipeline, an index, and access to the relevant context. Similarity can help narrow an investigation; it does not establish a root cause by itself.

Figure 10. Time-series embeddings can support a search for similar patterns across equipment and other signals.

The same models and building blocks can support different workflows across industries:.

According to recent reports, figure 11. The plant twin, from sensor to setpoint. A new cream lot pulls overrun off target. The forecast reads the line, the agent proposes a new draw temperature and air flow, the operator approves, and the tubs are back in spec. Simulated data.

Figure 12. The store twin, a store and its supply chain. A promo is coming for oat milk. The forecast prices in the promo and sets the reorder point, the agent raises a purchase order, the planner approves, and the shelf is full on promo day. Simulated data.

According to recent reports, banking: payments and the trading desk. The fraud lead wants to stop card testing without blocking good customers, and the trader wants a large order done without moving the price. Every card and every symbol is scored against its own expected pattern, event by event. Fraud and security holds the odd swipe before authorization, anomaly detection spots the unusual flow, and trading paces each order with the forecast volume.

Airlines: hub operations, fleet and network. Operations control wants to see a disruption coming while there is still time to act. Engine, gate and network streams are forecast and checked in real time. Anomaly detection catches the engine reading that drifts, production optimization rebalances gates and crews, and supply chain planning puts the spare part where the aircraft will be.

In every industry, the Streamhouse does the same work: Flink runs the Granite models to forecast, detect and optimize, Streaming Agents act on the live context, and people approve the exceptions.

Explore the models on Confluent to see how time-series intelligence can support real-time decisions.

Amazon DynamoDB vector search now supports new inline filter operators

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (228 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, amazon DynamoDB vector search inline filters now support range comparisons, value lists, and logical operators in addition to the equality operator, so you can narrow a vector search to exactly the items you want.
  • The search condition expression in a SearchVectors request now accepts the comparison operators <, <=, >, >=, and BETWEEN on Number attributes, the IN operator, the attribute_exists and attribute_not_exists functions, and the logical operators AND, OR, and NOT.
  • The new operators are available in all AWS Regions where DynamoDB vector search is available.

In a recent development, amazon DynamoDB vector search inline filters now support range comparisons, value lists, and logical operators in addition to the equality operator, so you can narrow a vector search to exactly the items you want. You can now filter on numeric ranges such as price, rating, or publish date, match an attribute against a list of values, check whether an attribute exists, and combine conditions with OR and NOT. Amazon DynamoDB vector indexes store vector embeddings alongside your operational data, and the SearchVectors API returns the items whose embeddings are most similar to your query vector.

The search condition expression in a SearchVectors request now accepts the comparison operators <, <=, >, >=, and BETWEEN on Number attributes, the IN operator, the attribute_exists and attribute_not_exists functions, and the logical operators AND, OR, and NOT. DynamoDB applies the filter during the search, so every result it returns matches. For example, a retail application can return the products most similar to a shopper's query within a price range and a set of brands, and a retrieval-augmented generation application can limit results to selected document categories published after a given date.

The new operators are available in all AWS Regions where DynamoDB vector search is available.

To learn more, see vector search in the Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide, or visit the Amazon DynamoDB page.

Breaking: Reconstructing risk preferences from data

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (142 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.27692v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the problem of reconstructing risk preferences from data. Specifically, for a finite dataset consisting of contingent claims and their evaluations, we aim at reconstructing a risk measure that is finite-valued, cash-additive, convex, and Lipschitz continuous. Our first result establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for a dataset to be compatible with a risk measure, that is the evaluations are stemming from a risk measure applied to the contingent claims. Our second result provides a reconstruction formula for compatible datasets, which we term \emph{universal risk measure}. We further extend the reconstruction to monotone risk measures and establish sharp Lipschitz constants for both general and monotone reconstructions. We further show that we explicitly reconstruct linear preferences and evaluations by the Expected Shortfall. We conclude with a numerical application to European options.

What a billion-dollar deal indicates about the US battery market

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (662 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US.
  • Sources indicate that sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries.
  • This arrangement also shows how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US.

Sources indicate that sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries. It’s a deal that Sila says could be worth more than $1 billion over time.

This arrangement also shows how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately. A major part of the financial backing for this factory’s production is a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department. While batteries can be a major tool to help drive the energy transition and cut emissions, right now much of the industry is more focused on geopolitics.

Founded in 2011, Sila makes silicon-based anodes for lithium-ion batteries. The big selling point here is the potential to improve energy density—Sila’s anode weighs a fifth as much as the graphite used in anodes today and cuts the volume in half, according to the company. So using this fresh material enables batteries to pack more energy into the same weight and volume, allowing longer range for EVs, for example. The material can also deliver more power and recharge faster, compared with conventional chemistry.

It has been revealed that we’ve been following Sila (and its competitors) for years. My colleague James Temple covered the company when its battery first appeared in Whoop fitness wearables in 2021.

Sources indicate that things have gotten a lot bigger since then. In 2022, Sila revealed plans for a factory in Moses Lake, Washington, and received $100 million from the US Department of Energy, part of a multibillion-dollar round of grants under the Biden administration to support the US battery supply chain.

In a recent development, the company opened its factory in September 2025, and it’s already operating. But the deal with Panasonic will help it scale to at least 10 times more production than current levels, states Gene Berdichevsky, the company’s cofounder and CEO.

Panasonic has committed to buying tens of thousands of tons of material, Berdichevsky says, though Sila isn’t sharing specific numbers on the total commitment or the price Panasonic is paying.

This agreement is Sila’s first mass-market deal and a substantial one for the United States’ next-generation battery market, which has largely been on the ropes over the past few years. Two billion-dollar battery companies, 24M and ESS Tech, have declared bankruptcy and shut down just in the last year.

The glimmer of hope here is tied up with something I’ve been noticing about this industry: the shifting politics. While batteries used to be firmly considered a climate technology, we’ve seen a lot of companies move away from messaging around the clean energy transition and lean into geopolitics.

Industry observers note that china dominates the battery world and particularly the battery anode market, controlling over 90% of graphite production today. For years, the US has been trying to curb reliance on Chinese batteries, battery materials, and other materials used in crucial technologies, like rare earth metals. But the Trump administration has ramped things up, and earlier this year the US Defense Department committed a $1.4 billion loan to Sila aimed at helping the US face a “significant technology sovereignty challenge,” as a press release put it.

In a recent development, sila’s announcement of the Panasonic deal does mention EVs—but not climate, emissions or the energy transition. Rather, it’s all about American industrialization. (And, of course, a mention that a North American battery supply chain can also help power the AI market.).

I asked Berdichevsky about this shift and whether the company holds decarbonization as a priority.

Industry observers note that “I think the politics of it has shifted around us much more than our motivations have shifted,” he said. “It’s really the energy efficiency that motivates engineers like myself and technologists at our organization. And I still think that that’s still at the heart of it.”.

A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1040 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering.
  • The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.
  • In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering.

The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.

In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System.

“Our group is the only one in the world to have maintained a human liver under fully normothermic, physiological conditions for seven weeks,” he notes.

Recent findings suggest that normothermic means body temperature, or about 37 °C. The previous record for keeping an internal organ alive outside the body was set in Switzerland several years ago. That organ—also a liver—lasted around two weeks.

Most organs destined for transplant survive only a few hours in special ice buckets and need to be raced to their destination. Over the last decade, however, surgeons have been switching to perfusion systems, which pump warm or cold fluids into an organ. This can double the time it can be held before it must be transplanted.

Pulitano states the key to breaking the record was to automate the systems used to keep the organ thriving. During a meeting in Switzerland earlier this year, the Sydney team described perfusing 55 human livers, one after the other. Some were connected to a system that needed to be adjusted manually, but for those placed on the automated system—which produced the seven-week survivor—the average survival time tripled, to about four weeks.

According to recent reports, perfusion has already enabled doctors to restart hearts from dead people and keep them beating outside the body. Paulo Martins, a transplant doctor at the University of Oklahoma, claims about half the kidneys he transplants are now perfused, even though the process can add $100,000 to the cost of a transplant.

While the research awaits formal publication, the eventual goal is what Pulitano and colleagues call “time-unlimited liver preservation.”.

Sources indicate that scientists have already discovered possible medical benefits to keeping organs on life support longer than usual. One, they say, is that perfused organs apparently start to repair themselves and become stronger after a day or so. That’s what led a Swiss team, in 2022, to transplant a damaged liver that had been kept on perfusion for three days—the longest time any internal organ had remained outside the body before a successful transplant, notes Waldemar Hoffmann, the CEO and cofounder of Apersys, a startup formed to commercialize the technology.

Pulitano says his own startup, Aeternum Life Technologies, will be helping with a planned trial in Sydney to transplant low-quality livers kept on perfusion for four days.

Industry observers note that what’s less clear, states Hoffmann, is whether any transplant surgeon would ever want, or need, to use an organ kept alive for nearly two months. He says people in the field believe Pulitano’s record is real, but they don’t know how healthy the organ was at the end or even what so much extra time is likely to achieve. “The key question is what the purpose for a seven-week perfusion would be,” he says.

Recent findings suggest that yet that’s where things could start to get interesting, says Martins, the Oklahoma surgeon. Long-term life support could enable far-out concepts like artificial wombs, upcoming types of organ manufacturing, and the chance to experiment directly on human organs outside the body for extended periods.

For his part, Pulitano states long-term machine perfusion could help grow fresh organs. In living donations, surgeons commonly take half of a person’s liver to give someone else. After about two months, both parts will have grown back almost to their full volume. Pulitano says he’s tried dividing a liver and then attaching the sections to the machine. If that works, he says, it could be a way to multiply one donor liver into several full-size organs.

According to recent reports, “It’s important to have people thinking outside the box and pushing the limits and creating possibilities for things that, right now, sometimes we don’t even have a need for but are going to be needed in the future,” says Martins. “That’s how science moves.”.

He’s not the only one who thinks so. For instance, a US company, Bexorg, has been reanimating human brains using perfusion pumps. The idea is to study what effects experimental drugs have on them. That company perfuses brains for about a day but has stated it wants to extend the time to two weeks.

Similar experiments can be done on livers, states Pulitano, who has already tried adding gene therapies to the organs. “It gives us a living human organ model for translational research that no animal system can match, because the biology, the immunology, and the drug responses are human from the outset,” he says.

In a recent development, meanwhile, in Silicon Valley, patents filed by Altos Labs, a billionaire-backed longevity startup, describe attempts to introduce reprogramming genes into animal livers maintained outside the body. Eventually, Altos scientists have speculated, they might temporarily disconnect a failing organ while it’s still in a person’s body, connecting it to a perfusion machine in order to douse it with ultra-powerful genetic treatments without risking the rest of the body.

Sources indicate that doctors probing the limits of organ life support have now formed two latest scientific societies to explore the concept. One, founded by Martins and called the International Society for Organ Preservation and Perfusion Therapy, will hold its inaugural meeting this year in Italy. The other, based in China, was launched in August to advance what doctors at the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-Sen University have termed “organ medicine”: research at the level of whole organs kept alive by “bionic maintenance.”.

Recent findings suggest that “What is exploding is the idea of this technology that clearly goes beyond simply organ preservation,” states Pulitano. “Basically, that’s a concept that’s entirely upcoming.”.

Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1401 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.
  • A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models.
  • GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.

A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models. The full version will be on arXiv soon.

GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That proposal is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move.

Better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It notes nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon.

We wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors.

The short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs.

According to recent reports, for a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time:.

Recent findings suggest that here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance.

It has been revealed that this is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O.

It has been revealed that these overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart.

To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range.

We treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded.

Two design choices shaped the work:.

Recent findings suggest that we compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost. Feature selection combined correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features.

Distribution of end-to-end duration across the 272 runs. Mean 23.43 h, median 15.29 h.

All numbers come from stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The first four rows are analytical and involve no fitting.

No single MFU value fixes the FLOP baseline. We swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65. The best setting, 30%, still leaves a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average.

Recent findings suggest that A more detailed analytical model does not close the gap. As a second baseline we took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work. It builds an explicit layer graph and accounts for compute, memory traffic and inter-device communication. We extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still correspond to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time. That says nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. It highlights how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step.

It has been revealed that linear models help, and then stall. Ridge brings MAE down to 7.23 h. The relationship between configuration and duration is not well captured by a purely linear model.

It has been revealed that gradient boosting does the heavy lifting. CatBoost and XGBoost land within one standard deviation of each other on every metric. We carry CatBoost forward because it has the lowest mean error across the board.

According to recent reports, catBoost's feature importance concentrates in a handful of features. Model and workload variables are there, as expected, but so are evaluation and checkpoint variables. num_eval_data, the total number of samples processed in evaluation over the life of the job, ranks first, followed by num_trainable_params, batch_eval_size_percent, num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent, with num_params_saved close behind. SHAP values tell the same story: high evaluation volume consistently pushes the predicted time up, while trainable parameter count has a nonlinear effect that only becomes large for the biggest models.

Mean feature importance of the CatBoost model across folds (PredictionValuesChange).

Feature importance is not a causal claim. Still, the pattern lines up with how a job is actually spent. How often you evaluate, how large the evaluation set is and how many checkpoints you persist all shape the wall-clock time, alongside model and dataset scale. These are choices people often make by habit when writing a training config.

Recent findings suggest that one caveat on reading the plots: larger GPU allocations show positive contributions to predicted time. In our data, bigger allocations go with bigger jobs, so num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale. It does not mean adding GPUs makes a job slower.

Recent findings suggest that looking at all 272 out-of-fold predictions, the median absolute error is 0.51 h. 80% of predictions are within 2.20 h and 90% are within 4.31 h. Broken down by job duration:.

In a recent development, up to 60 hours, the median error stays at about one hour or less. The long tail is where the model struggles, and with only 13 runs above 60 hours we read that as a data limitation.

It has been revealed that out-of-fold absolute error against real duration, colored by duration range. Errors stay low up to 60 h and widen in the sparse tail.

More data should still help. On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE drops from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when going from 85% to 100% of the training partition, with no clear plateau.

In practice, the predictor gives a scheduler a duration it can blueprint around before a job starts: which jobs to run together, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will finish in time for its deadline.

What does transfer is the method: overhead-aware features, multicollinearity-aware selection and the comparison protocol. The full paper will report the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters in full, so the pipeline can be rebuilt on any execution-log dataset with a similar structure.

Next on our list: hardware-specific descriptors and validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for configurations with few observations, other training objectives, and more data on long runs.

Sources indicate that the full paper is coming to arXiv soon. Follow the Dharma-AI organization on Hugging Face to be notified when it is out, and leave your questions in the comments below. We would like to hear how you estimate job duration on your own clusters.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (201 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

arXiv:2611.27616v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tools from econophysics, including Random Matrix Theory (RMT), Tsallis q-Gaussian tails, Hawkes self-excitation and diffusion-inspired regularization, are often proposed as ingredients for financial risk models, but their incremental value over strong contemporary benchmarks remains unclear. We introduce a Physics-Inspired Neural Covariance (PINC) framework for one-day-ahead covariance forecasting using 1-minute data from the 29 Dow Jones Industrial Average constituents over 545 trading days. The model incorporates RMT-cleaned correlations, Tsallis tail indices and Hawkes intensities as inputs and optionally includes a Fokker-Planck-inspired regularization term selected strictly on validation data. Evaluation is performed through a nested walk-forward design with 11 folds, 231 out-of-sample trading days and multiple random seeds, with explicit leakage controls and reproducibility tests. Neural models outperform static covariance estimators such as sample, Ledoit-Wolf, RMT and EVT-based estimators, but show no statistically significant improvement over HAR-RV or LSTM benchmarks. Validation consistently rejects the physics-inspired regularizer, and ablation studies find no measurable contribution from the RMT, Tsallis or Hawkes features. Portfolio experiments show no statistically significant Sharpe ratio improvement after transaction costs. These results suggest that, for this dataset and forecasting horizon, econophysics-inspired components do not provide measurable benefits beyond strong financial forecasting benchmarks.

Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive on life support outside the body for seven weeks, smashing the previous record of about two weeks.

They achieved the feat by connecting a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.

The approach could open up new possibilities in biomedical engineering, from repairing damaged organs to growing new ones. Some researchers are even exploring artificial wombs.

Take a closer look at the technology keeping human organs alive.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, today, Amazon CloudWatch confirms support for your own application telemetry in the CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on.
  • In a recent development, applications instrumented with an OpenTelemetry SDK send to an OTLP endpoint that the agent serves on every node, on by default.
  • In a recent development, for Prometheus metrics, the agent scrapes the targets described by standard ServiceMonitor and PodMonitor objects, with no Prometheus operator to run and no change to your scrape configuration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, today, Amazon CloudWatch confirms support for your own application telemetry in the CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on. The CloudWatch agent you already run now accepts metrics, traces, and logs from your applications, so you don't deploy and operate a separate collector to get them into CloudWatch.

In a recent development, applications instrumented with an OpenTelemetry SDK send to an OTLP endpoint that the agent serves on every node, on by default. Metrics arrive as CloudWatch metrics you query with PromQL, traces go to AWS X-Ray and Transaction Search, and logs go to CloudWatch Logs.

In a recent development, for Prometheus metrics, the agent scrapes the targets described by standard ServiceMonitor and PodMonitor objects, with no Prometheus operator to run and no change to your scrape configuration. Each team defines its own targets alongside its application rather than in one central add-on configuration. Label selectors let you choose which monitors CloudWatch scrapes.

Both sources carry the same Kubernetes, host, cloud, and service attributes the add-on applies to the pod they came from, so you can join application telemetry to your cluster metrics.

Custom telemetry is available in version 8.0.0 and later of the EKS add-on and Helm chart, in all AWS Regions where CloudWatch supports OpenTelemetry metrics. Telemetry is charged at the Amazon EKS OpenTelemetry ingestion rate of $0.08 per GB. For details, see Amazon CloudWatch insights pricing.

To get started, see Custom telemetry in the Amazon CloudWatch User Guide.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0:.

The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window. The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings.

We recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats.

After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000, you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client:.

The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content, and its final answer in content. These settings follow the model card’s quickstart.

DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%.

Sources indicate that scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings.

Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes.

We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set.

We selected tasks using three criteria:.

It has been revealed that radixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

Recent findings suggest that 57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

Sources indicate that stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

In a recent development, every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs.

Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded.

Our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently.

According to recent reports, the service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%.

Cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine.

Download DaisyRose-27B, follow the SGLang serving guide, or use Miles to train your own agents.

We’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab.

We thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.

arXiv:2611.27505v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An AI-assisted payment can pass assessment and lose release authority before commitment. We specify a banking delegation contract that checks current authority, the shared payment cap and the capacity of eligible instruments to cover losses. It books the new payment and its recovery demands and writes the outcome record in the same atomic transition. A paired example identifies the authorised mandate, applied rule and selection inputs a reviewer needs to assess mandate conformance. We show that, under fixed resource inputs, the transition preserves the payment cap and recovery feasibility when commitments and effective withdrawals are ordered against the same authoritative state. Reversing a transmitted priority changes the selected route in 4 of 32 distinct behavioural combinations, represented by 96 of 576 labelled contexts. The executor follows the transmitted rule in all of them. Reusing earlier state admits 23 releases in 123 histories blocked by the reference. Pooling recovery capacity admits 69 infeasible configurations in a grid of 576. Both current-state implementations agree with the reference in all 144 commitment histories and 624 concurrent schedules. The retention test recovers five specified outcome fields from each of 47 complete records. Fifteen survey responses informed requirements for resolving holds and handling uncertain delivery. An insurance example illustrates referral after an adverse coverage finding.

  • Data Hub (preview) is available in the US East (N.

Today, AWS confirms the preview of Data Hub in AWS Billing and Cost Management, a managed data layer that enables AWS FinOps Agent to query cost and usage data with SQL. In preview, Data Hub is available to AWS FinOps Agent, so the agent can identify the individual resources behind a cost change, break down spend by team or cost allocation tag, and show how a resource's cost and usage change hour by hour. With AWS FinOps Agent and Data Hub, customers get these answers without setting up a data export or building and maintaining a cost data pipeline.

In a recent development, data Hub provides 13 months of hourly, resource-level cost and usage data in the published CUR 2.0 schema, including resource identifiers and cost allocation tags. AWS provisions the data, refreshes data daily, and maintains the schema as fresh services, commitments, and charge types are added. When set up from the management account, Data Hub covers cost and usage data across the accounts in your organization.

Data Hub (preview) is available in the US East (N. Virginia) Region and covers cost and usage data across regions. There is no charge for Data Hub during preview.

Sources indicate that to learn more about Data Hub, see the AWS Billing and Cost Management User Guide and the launch blog. You can get started from the Data Hub page in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console or from the AWS FinOps Agent console.

Tech Report: Risk sharing for background risk models with infinite mean

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (170 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.27485v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: Risk sharing is usually viewed as beneficial for risk-averse agents facing independent risks with finite means, but this situation can be reversed for infinite-mean losses. In this paper, we explore the effects of risk sharing for positively dependent infinite-mean losses using background risk models. Under both linear and conditional mean risk sharing, we show that risk sharing of infinite-mean losses can increase the risk in the sense of usual stochastic order. Our results cover classical multivariate loss distributions, including the Pareto-Clayton and the Fr\'echet-Gumbel models. For linear risk sharing, we further derive stochastic dominance relations between diversified portfolios, including those with Pareto marginals coupled by convex mixtures of commonly used Archimedean copulas. For conditional mean risk sharing, we additionally discuss peakedness and stochastic order relations for stable distributions. Consequently, under the stated conditions, retaining the original risk or a less diversified portfolio is preferred under every law-invariant monotone risk measure that is well defined for infinite-mean models.

#26232. Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3834 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3834 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.
  • Industry observers note that models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing.
  • In a recent development, take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.

Industry observers note that models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination.

In a recent development, take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time.

Our earlier work (multi-harness RL, harness adapters) showed that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations.

We leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6. The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol:.

Industry observers note that most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop, SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM's agent and environment classes, slime's custom rollout functions, or ART's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer.

Industry observers note that for this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv. We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains.

Sources indicate that RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything.

This section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate, and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B.

Sources indicate that each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves:.

Sources indicate that we used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest.

A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials:.

Each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task:.

Industry observers note that 858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded.

A valid task can still teach nothing. GRPO (group relative policy optimization) scores each attempt against the other attempts at the same task, so a task where every attempt passes, or every attempt fails, gives no learning signal. Before training, Qwen3.8-27B attempted each task 4 times, or 8 times for a stratified sample of six tasks per repository.

In a recent development, of 442 scored tasks, Qwen3.8-27B solved 151 every time and 120 never. The 171 tasks it solved only sometimes form the qualified set. The figure below shows how the scores pile up at both ends and how they differ by source. The model solves most Go tasks every time, fails every attempt on more than a third of the SWE-smith Python tasks, and lands in the middle on 73% of the SWE-Gym tasks.

Qwen3.8-27B results on 442 scored tasks. Green marks the qualified tasks, which the model solves on some attempts but not all.

According to recent reports, this example demonstrates how we filtered and validated 1,127 tasks to 278 which we included directly in the final dataset. The pipeline then took the remaining 522 rejected tasks, repaired and complexified them with Tasksmith and repeated validation.

Recent findings suggest that the pipeline applies two filters: validation removes broken tasks, and the difficulty check keeps tasks the base model solves only sometimes. This section tests whether those filters change what the model learns. We trained four short runs of up to 50 steps, each on tasks from a different stage of the pipeline, and compared them with the base model on Terminal-Bench 2.1.

Each run trains Qwen3.8-27B with LoRA and GRPO, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, on 32 tasks. All four use the same agent harness (OpenCode with up to 48 model calls), the same settings and one 8×H200 Hugging Face Job, and the reward is the verifier's pass or fail. The task sets differ in how they were filtered:.

Industry observers note that the figure below indicates how the tasks impacted model learning. The table lists each run's steps and the checkpoint we evaluate. The chart tracks training reward across subsets of tasks with differing validation status.

harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories. Hub tasks are capped at 40 per repository, so no single project dominates. The table below highlights what each source contributes. The dataset has two views: every accepted task, and the qualified subset for GRPO training. Rejected attempts stay in a separate config.

We leveraged the stable version of AsyncGRPOTrainer from TRL, with the main advantage of the trainer being that it does not wait until all rollouts are completed before moving to the next training optimization step.

For more detailed reading on the trainer and its building blocks, please refer to the AsyncGRPO blogpost.

To obtain our final harness adapters, we trained LoRA adapters on top of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer. The adapters were attached to the model using the all-linear flag. To maximize the training efficiency, thinking mode was turned off during rollout stages, and we evaluated our final adapter with and without thinking for broader comparison.

The final reward function consists of the verifier's correctness, combined with a small tool-efficiency bonus (0.1, derived from early experiments from the previous iteration of harness adapters which indicated that 0.1 worked best).

According to recent reports, we performed a small LR sweep on 50 steps using Termgrade environments (1e-5, 5e-5 and 1e-4) and noticed that 1e-5 barely moved training correctness (from 0.52 to 0.50), 1e-4 collapsed the rollouts instead of improving them (turns per rollout moved from 18 to 6, with entropy rising), and only 5e-5 clearly improved (from 0.49 to 0.60 by step 40). Longer 5e-5 runs then showed signs of instability (collapsing rollout lengths, rising entropy), so we settled on 2e-5 for the final runs.

Recent findings suggest that each harness adapter was trained using NVIDIA 2xB200 GPUs, with one GPU allocated for the vLLM server and the other allocated for the training process. We first performed some stress testing to maximize the amount of RL tasks that can be trained within a single optimization step. For that, we ‘maxed out’ the --token-budget argument from AsyncGRPOTrainer to its limit for the setup that we had. The chart below shows the evolution of the number of groups per step for each harness (in blue: Pi, green: OpenCode and orange: Hermes).

As the model gets better and better during training, it is able to fit more and more groups during each training step, which diversifies the signals that the model gets at each optimization step.

Sources indicate that the final data mixture consists of 750 tasks from harness-adapters RL environments and 300 tasks from termgrade. In order to maximize the diversity of the sampled tasks during training, we have slightly customized the data sampling strategy, which will be explained below:.

Before training, the tasks are put in a fixed order that interleaves them by family (i.e., their repository for our generated RL environments. For Termgrade, we just sorted them by name since each task is considered as its own family), so every training step mixes as many repositories as possible while following the distribution of the mixture.

Recent findings suggest that we also plug the safeagents tool, in order to block any misbehavior from the model during training. The final plugin (which consists of the regex and pattern rules specific to the RL tasks and test path) is hosted in harness-hub/qwen-safeagents-plugin and can be used out of the box using the latest version of safeagents in case anyone wants to reproduce the training setup.

It has been revealed that the number of blocked tools from safeagents decreases consistently during training, which indicates that the model gets ‘safer and safer’ after each optimization step. Below is a diagram of the safeagents blocked calls per 1000 tool calls, by training step, for each harness adapter.

Merging models often combines their capabilities while keeping most of what each one could do. Once the three harness adapters were trained, we asked two questions. Does merging them cost accuracy? And can a single "super-adapter" be accurate and efficient under every harness?

Industry observers note that we started by comparing the weight updates of the three adapters, layer by layer. The cosine similarity between any two of them is about 0.01–0.02: each adapter pushed the model in a nearly orthogonal direction during training. That's the best case for merging, since the updates barely interfere.

Industry observers note that we concatenate the three LoRA adapters along the rank dimension (PEFT's combination_type="cat"). The merged adapter has rank 96 (3 × 32) and applies exactly w · (ΔW_pi + ΔW_hermes + ΔW_opencode). Prior work on merging (task arithmetic, TIES, KnOTS) finds that scaling each revision below 1 works best, so we compared three weights on all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, under each harness, with the step-120 adapters:.

The plain sum over-applies the updates. The agents become very short (13 tool calls per task, against 49 for the base model), and while Hermes peaks at 62.8%, pi falls back to the base model's level. The average dilutes each harness's own revision. ½ gives the best balance, so we built the final super-adapter from the released checkpoints (pi step 160, hermes step 160, opencode step 150) at weight ½.

Under each harness, on the tasks every run graded (50–51 on SWE-bench Pro, 82–85 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), one attempt per task (in parentheses, the efficiency gain with respect to the base model):.

"Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default effort (xhigh). The specialists were trained and served with thinking off.

With thinking off, the super-adapter improves on the base model on all six harness–benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 39.5% → 49.0%; 71 tasks newly solved vs 34 lost, p < 0.001).

Despite not being trained at all with thinking on, it's the strongest model we evaluated with thinking mode. Against the base model thinking at the same effort, it wins on five of six pairs and ties the sixth (mean 55.5% → 63.5%; 67 newly solved vs 37 lost, p = 0.004). The largest gains are on SWE-bench Pro: +16 points under hermes and +20 under opencode. Under pi on SWE-bench Pro, where thinking alone already reaches 74%, it ties.

In a recent development, use the specialist harness adapters when thinking off. Each harness's own adapter is ahead on four of six pairs, by the most under pi (64.0% vs 46.0% on SWE-bench Pro, 56.5% vs 48.2% on Terminal-Bench). Splitting one model across three harnesses costs pi the most of its gain. If you only use one harness and keep thinking off, take its specialist.

The super adapter is also much more efficient. On the tasks both the base model and the super-adapter solve, with thinking off, it makes 53–73% fewer tool calls and generates 44–60% fewer tokens per task, with fewer tool calls on 111 of 130 tasks. With thinking on, it still cuts tool calls by 31–48% and tokens by 24–43% on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench, tool calls drop by 19–25% and token counts stay about the same.

Recent findings suggest that the ½ weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the step-120 adapters, so the Terminal-Bench numbers are slightly optimistic; SWE-bench Pro played no part in the choice. Full paired results are in the super-adapter's model card.

This section reports what happened during training, then how the adapters score on held-out benchmarks inside and outside their own harnesses.

Training ran for a cumulative total of 598 steps, with a total of 78,114 samples trained, which consists exactly of 167M trained tokens.

Recent findings suggest that during training, we see a clear signal that the model learns to solve tasks in fewer and fewer steps, with no clear sign of saturation. Despite having some clear increasing trend sometimes, training correctness seems to overall stay flat. This can be explained by the fact that the model meets newly introduced tasks during training, but the number of groups that fit in a step’s token budget more than doubles as trajectories get shorter. The accuracy gains show up on the held-out benchmarks in the section below.

On the other hand, safeagents was able to block multiple suspicious attempts. Across the three training runs, a total of 1.3M tool calls have been checked, and a total of 647 tool calls have been blocked.

This section covers the evaluation setup, the in-harness results, transfer across harnesses, and an out-of-distribution check.

According to recent reports, we evaluate each adapter inside the harness it was trained in, on two agentic coding benchmarks: all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 (1 hour and 100 agent steps per task) and the 51 hardest tasks of SWE-bench Pro (2 hours and 100 agent steps). We cap the maximum number of tokens per task to be 131072. We do not tune the agent settings and use the default setup for all harnesses. For example, Pi automatically applies context compaction, while OpenCode and Hermes don't, which mainly affects the SWE-bench Pro results due to rapid context overflow. Therefore you cannot compare the results across different harnesses (using Pi does not necessarily lead to better results than Hermes or OpenCode), but it is fair to compare results within the same harness and draw conclusions.

Every rollout runs through the same Harbor and OpenEnv stack as training, in HF sandboxes, with one attempt per task at temperature 0.8 and thinking off. Each LoRA checkpoint is merged into the base weights and served alone with vLLM on a single GPU, at the same concurrency as the base model's eval.

For all the evaluation benchmarks, we report the pass@1 as well as the number of tool calls, total turns, for all tasks and for solved tasks.

For openness, all model trajectories for final evaluations are pushed in this public bucket: harness-hub/harness-adapters-trajectories.

Recent findings suggest that all three specialist adapters beat the base model under their own harness, on both benchmarks. On SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), pi goes from 39.2% to 64.7% (+25.5 points: 15 tasks newly solved vs 2 lost, p = 0.002), hermes from 29.4% to 43.1%, and opencode from 35.3% to 51.0%. On the full Terminal-Bench 2.1, pi gains +16.3 points (16 vs 2, p = 0.001) and hermes +14.1 (19 vs 7, p = 0.03). Opencode gains +6.0 overall, and +13.6 on the 66 tasks that played no part in choosing its checkpoint (12 vs 3, p = 0.035).

The adapters also solve tasks much more efficiently: on the tasks both they and the base model solve, they make 56–72% fewer tool calls per task on SWE-bench Pro and 53–70% fewer on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The single super-adapter beats the base model under all three harnesses too (+6 to +18 points on SWE-bench Pro, +5 to +10 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), with just as large a cut in tool calls (53–73%). It keeps less of each specialist's gain with thinking off, most under pi, but with thinking on it beats the base model thinking at the same effort on five of six harness–benchmark pairs (see the super-adapter section). Each model card has the full paired results.

To answer this question, we also evaluated the pi harness adapter under Hermes Agent and OpenCode.

According to recent reports, under OpenCode it matches OpenCode's own specialist on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (44.8% → 54.0%, against 46.4% → 52.4%). Under Hermes it keeps about two-thirds of the specialist's gain (46.3% → 56.1%, against 44.7% → 58.8%), with the same ~45% cut in tool calls in both. Therefore it seems that the newly learned capabilities are transferred across harnesses.

What happens if we evaluate in out-of-distribution tasks, outside the harnesses the adapters have been trained with?

Sources indicate that we ran all five models on 300 AutomationBench tasks which consists of business-automation workflows evaluations, with AutomationBench's own agent loop instead of Pi, Hermes or OpenCode. This way, we can cross check two different questions: can the model solve problems outside SWE-related tasks? What happens when the model is being put outside the harness it has been trained with?

Results show that the adapters stay close to the base model. Pi and OpenCode are slightly ahead (27.0% and 25.3% pass@1 against 23.0%), the merged adapter is level (23.7%), and Hermes is a few points behind (17.7%). The differences are within noise, except perhaps Hermes, therefore RL inside the harnesses neither transfers clearly to this very different setting nor breaks the model on it.

We appreciate the feedback from the users and the community, initial testing and results from the community seemed overall extremely positive, and we wish to continue in this direction in the future. We also saw some surprising results, such as users reporting that the harness adapters work really well under Qwen3.8 derivatives, such as Swift-1.5.

This question is an open question we thought about, post-release. After inspecting carefully the generated trajectories from the evaluation benchmarks, it turns out the model, under non-thinking mode, tends to generate some short text before proposing a tool call, as opposed to the base model which generates the tool calls barely without any text beforehand.

This phenomenon can be seen as a sort of ‘reasoning leakage’, where the model learns to ‘escape’ from its non-thinking version to its thinking version by generating some text that can sometimes look like reasoning traces (e.g.: ..wait? ..let me see, etc.). A recent paper also describes behavior from LLMs during the RL stage very well.

Does this invalidate our models? We do not think so, as the final results are still valid; under the exact same conditions (fixed token budget) our adapters do outperform the base non-thinking model (by far) and match the performance of the thinking version, while being much more token efficient. This has been further confirmed by the positive feedback from the community.

According to recent reports, however this raises the need of a proper follow up work, where we will try to re-apply the same pipeline for pure thinking models, as well as exploring hybrid thinking / non-thinking training, to better understand the behavior of RL training on hybrid thinking models. We will share with the community our next findings (and harness adapters), once we get conclusive results.

It has been revealed that throughout this work, we demonstrated that RL training your model inside your target harness leads to more efficient and therefore more accurate final models, when evaluated under the same conditions. This observation is in line and in continuation with several previous work from Hugging Face teams, such as multi-harness-RL or the early iterations of harness adapters.

In the future, we will explore applying this recipe to more models, while better studying the training strategies for hybrid thinking / non-thinking models.

It has been revealed that we also share to the community openly the full recipe and pipeline to reproduce everything, and invite everyone to build their own RL tasks, derived from their own codebase, or any relevant materials, and apply the same training recipe and ideas to their favorite model and harness for more efficient agentic models. We hope this blogpost will serve as a starting point for builders to build and share their own harness adapters in the future.

Thanks for such a nice and detailed blog on it. Can you also share, how many iterations did this take, and roughly how long end to end? What would be the minimum GPU requirements to train. Also curious how you think the adapter holds up when the harness changes.

Nice article guys!For adapters merging, one cool idea would be to do MOPD where the student is Qwen3.8-27B (the original one) and teachers are the RL lora adapted one. The random selection of the harness selects the teacher.
