📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why Netflixâs $82B Acquisition Makes Sense in the Era of AI.

Why Netflixâs $82B Acquisition Makes Sense in the Era of AI.

Netflix recently entered into a definitive agreement to buy Warner Brothers for over $82B in Enterprise Value. Itâs being called the biggest, most consequential deal in Hollywood history. The purchase comes with intellectual property including Batman, Superman, Harry Potter, Game of Thrones, The Significant Bang Theory, The Sopranos, The Matrix, Lord of the Rings (film rights), Godzilla/MonsterVerse, Mad Max, and Mortal Kombat.

IP like this became more valuable in the internet age, and will become even more valuable in the age of AI. Earlier this year, I published an internal Sequoia memo detailing the implications of AI on the IP industry. Given the substantial news, I thought it would be nice to share a few excerpts with my friends and colleagues more broadly.

According to recent reports, on a recent work trip to Paris, a profound irony struck me at the MusÃ©e dâOrsay. The museum, a glorious former train station, is a temple to the Industrial Revolution. Its collection, spanning 1848 to 1914, chronicles the period of historyâs most rapid industrialization.

Edgar Degas: Course de Gentleman (Gentlemenâs Race).

The art is filled with tributes to this fresh age: Monet paints locomotives at La Gare Saint-Lazare, smokestacks fill the background of Degasâ Course de Gentlemen, and the Traders in factory-made clothing. It is a museum drenched in the dawn of industrialization.

Claude Monet: La Gare Saint-Lazare.

This is where the paradox lies. This was the exact moment in history when the cost to reproduce a piece of art dropped precipitously. What was once near-impossible, replicating a masterpiece, became trivially cheap. Logically, as near-perfect copies became ubiquitous, the value of the âoriginalâ should have plummeted. And yet, the opposite happened. The great lesson of the dâOrsay is this: instead of becoming worthless in the age of manufacturing, these original works became priceless. As reproduction became easy, the value and allure of the original only went up.

Edgar Degas: At the Stock Exchange.

Hereâs why IP is well positioned in an AI future:.

If we have AGI, or even inexpensive content creation, that will drive down the cost of intelligence.

That affordable intelligence will be used to create an abundance of content.

Humans will react to abundance with a desire for familiarity and quality.

The value of the âoriginalâ will only increase.

In this era, âoriginalâ works will increase in value quickly.

These âoriginalsâ include art, real estate, and intellectual property.

Intellectual property that has already earned a spot in our minds will benefit disproportionately.

In the AI Era, nostalgic content will benefit disproportionately as it is manifest in countless different ways.

In a recent development, as content production costs approach zero, the marginal cost of newly introduced content will also become negligible, leading to an explosion in content volume. This content flood will profoundly shift the value of attention, the primary currency in this new landscape. Undifferentiated content will rapidly lose value, and consumers will be far less willing to invest time in new content unless itâs algorithmically recommended by dominant platforms. Very few new content concepts will break out, following an extreme Power Law.

According to recent reports, success in this environment will hinge on âattention distribution,â defined as a consumerâs inherent interest in a specific piece of content. Nostalgic content is poised to become the most valuable. In a world saturated with novelty, authentic nostalgic content will be incredibly difficult to simulate accurately; even slight deviations from the original will feel inauthentic and cheap.

Industry observers note that consumers will be willing to pay for nostalgic content due to its relatively low cost. For parents, the decision to purchase authentic nostalgic content for their children over a knockoff, especially when the real item is priced reasonably, becomes a clear choice.

The Impending Content Deluge and the Scarcity of Attention.

Recent findings suggest that the ubiquity of General AI will drastically reduce the marginal cost of content production, approaching zero. This will unleash an unprecedented explosion in content volume, creating a hyper-saturated information environment. In this landscape, human attention, rather than content itself, will become the primary scarce resource and the dominant currency. Undifferentiated content, easily replicable and ubiquitous, will rapidly depreciate in value. Consumers, overwhelmed by choice, will increasingly rely on algorithmic recommendations from dominant content platforms to filter and curate their experiences, leading to a profound shift in content discovery and consumption patterns.

Attention Distribution: The New Competitive Moat.

In a recent development, success in this AI-driven content economy will hinge on âattention distribution,â defined as a consumerâs inherent and deeply ingrained interest in a specific piece of content. This is distinct from mere algorithmic visibility, as it speaks to an intrinsic desire to engage with content. While AI can generate novel content at scale, it will struggle to replicate the nuanced emotional resonance and deeply embedded cultural references that drive genuine attention.

The Inherent Value of Authentic Nostalgic Content.

Nostalgic content is uniquely positioned to become the most valuable asset in this future. The core arguments for its enduring value are:.

Difficulty of Authentic Simulation: While AGI can mimic styles and tropes, accurately simulating authentic nostalgic content will be incredibly challenging. The most popular feature in Sora 2 is their âCameoâ feature, which pulls in authentic characters and people into the AI generated worlds. Even minute deviations from the original, like a slight alteration in a beloved characterâs voice, a subtle anachronism in a period piece, or a deviation in the execution of a well-known narrative, will register as âinauthenticâ or âcheapâ to a discerning audience. The emotional connection to nostalgic content is often rooted in precise, well-remembered details, making it highly resistant to imperfect algorithmic replication. This is akin to the âuncanny valleyâ in robotics, where near-human but imperfect simulations evoke discomfort rather than acceptance.

Consumer Willingness to Pay: Despite the approaching zero marginal cost of content, consumers will demonstrate a significant willingness to pay for authentic nostalgic content.

Industry observers note that as AI democratizes content creation, the landscape will shift dramatically. The true scarcity will be human attention, and the ultimate value will reside in content that can capture and hold that attention through genuine emotional resonance. Authentic nostalgic content, by virtue of its irreplicable emotional depth and its proven ability to connect across generations, represents a highly defensible and appreciating asset in this evolving digital economy. Investors should prioritize companies that control and strategically leverage these invaluable cultural touchstones.

Breaking: Best Gifts for Mom (2026): Digital Wall Calendars, Better Bags, Personalized Jewelry, and More

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, moms give the best gifts, so it stands to reason that you should get the best gifts for Mom when you're shopping for her in any scenario.
  • Sources indicate that if you're worried you're going to give her a disappointing gift or something she already has, fear not: I've gathered the coolest things we recommend here at WIRED that just about any mom will love.
  • Updated November 2026: I've added Therabody's Theraface Mask Glo, Omnilux's Contour Gloves, WanderFull's HydroBag, and Nuuly's clothing subscription as new gifts to this guide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, moms give the best gifts, so it stands to reason that you should get the best gifts for Mom when you're shopping for her in any scenario. That includes Mother's Day, her birthday, Christmas, Hanukkah, or any other holiday in your family's life that includes gift-giving. The holiday season is now upon us, and I've added a few gift ideas with that time of year in mind.

Sources indicate that if you're worried you're going to give her a disappointing gift or something she already has, fear not: I've gathered the coolest things we recommend here at WIRED that just about any mom will love. From wellness gadgets that can improve her skin to the best tote bags I've tried, and even a device that puts her digital calendar in an IRL device, moms everywhere can get a ton out of these gifts. Many of these are items I've given to my mother, or other WIRED staffers have given to theirs. Or they might be at the top of my own wish list as a mother of a 4-year-old.

Updated November 2026: I've added Therabody's Theraface Mask Glo, Omnilux's Contour Gloves, WanderFull's HydroBag, and Nuuly's clothing subscription as new gifts to this guide.

Sources indicate that the must-have gadget for women of almost any age is an LED mask. These masks promise to use red light to erase wrinkles, brighten your skin, and keep acne at bay. I haven't seen much change in my wrinkles in my year-plus of regularly using a red-light mask, but I can confirm it makes my skin brighter and calms down acne and scars much faster when I'm regularly treating my skin, and I always get compliments on how nice my skin looks when I'm regularly using it. Therabody's TheraFace Mask Glo has a range of treatments with both red and blue light, a unique vibration therapy feature, and removable eye shields if you don't want the light in your eyes.

Look, nothing says mom life like looking for the perfect bag. I'm in a massive tote phase of my life; I somehow need to either lug an armload of items for myself and my son (or just myself!) or I only need a tiny belt bag. There's no in between.

It has been revealed that the Yardsale Day Bag has been my go-to for a variety of needs, from a colorful personal item for a flight to a gym bag to the aerial studio. It's got a waterproof bottom that makes me happy to bring it to the zoo's splash pad, and a magnetic middle separator you can flex to separate the middle of the bag into two medium sections to better divide all your items. Plus, there are a handful of side pockets inside, but none are large enough for my massive Owala water bottle. I have the 30L in Butter, but there's also a smaller 20L version if you're looking for something a little more compact.

Sources indicate that if your mom wants something a little more stylish, the Alex Mill totes are always on my mind. They come in a variety of gorgeous colors and are made of coated canvas, so they can put up with daily adventures, and you can customize them with your mom's initials (or even just the word “mom”!) with Alex Mill's hand-painted letter service. It's a simpler tote with no other pockets, but you can use the top snaps to let out the sides or tuck them in, depending on how much space Mom needs on a given day. The weathered color and vibe of these bags also feel perfect for the fall season.

Recent findings suggest that my latest favorite family planning gadget is a digital wall calendar. These handy devices take the Google Calendar I live by (and just about any other digital calendar, if your mom isn't a Google girl) and put it on a physical device I can promptly tap into without needing to grab my phone or bark at Alexa. The Skylight Calendar 2 is my favorite, because it not only includes to-do lists, meal planning, and a recipe book but also doubles as a digital photo frame. That means it displays cute photos of my family most of the time, and then, with a simple tap, it opens the calendar or whatever page I was last on to show me what's on my family's schedule. It does have a subscription fee, though, to get the digital photo frame feature and a few other options, like meal planning. But I think it's well worth it to get so many features in a single device. You can also gift her kiddo a Skylight Buddy ($140) so that she doesn't have to remind them to check the main calendar for their chores; it'll appear on their own device if they have a Buddy.

To me, motherhood is all about change. It's most obvious at the start of motherhood, when your body changes a lot over the course of nine months, but motherhood encompasses the rest of our lives, and our bodies and style change a lot over that time. One of the biggest giveaways that time has gone by is our clothes—how well they fit for our current stage, whether they reflect the time of our life right now, and if we're bored out of our skull with everything but don't want to buy an entirely latest closet.

In a recent development, I've been loving renting from Nuuly this pregnancy because the brand has an entire maternity section that lets me find pieces to fit me in this short—but very different size—season of my life. My older mother also loves having a clothing subscription because she gets bored of her outfit options to wear into the office, and I loved it for the same reason when I had my first clothing subscription right out of college. If Mom has been talking about wanting some upcoming looks but feels overwhelmed about what she wants to invest in, these rental services are a fun way to get a lot of new clothes in your life without having to store them or spend as much as you would have (some of my favorite maternity clothes I've gotten through Nuuly would have cost me $200 apiece!) The service costs $98 a month, but your first month is discounted to just $60. There's one piece I miss already that might drive me to pick up a second subscription, which would genuinely be cheaper than buying the piece I want brand new.

For years, the go-to gift for a woman in my family, mother or not, was shopping in the jewelry section of a department store. My mom even helped orchestrate this for the rest of the aunties and grandmas, but now, as a mom myself, I find myself interested in jewelry that tells a story about my family and children instead of just any old set. (Except extra earrings for my earring stack, a gift I'm thrilled to get, because there's never enough.).

According to recent reports, I love these pieces from Gorjana and BaubleBar that you can customize. Gorjana has a ton of charms you can add to its necklaces or bracelets to reflect Mom’s kids’ initials, birthstones, or anything else; I paired a charm of my son’s first initial ($50) with the Wilshire Adjustable Necklace ($68). If she's more of a ring gal, BaubleBar's Toi et Moi ring ($78) lets you choose two birthstones to display. I chose my and my son's birthstones, but luckily his sibling-to-be will also have a red birthstone, so it'll remain a perfect reflection of my kids and me for years to come.

This item was literally made for sports moms: a padded stadium cushion with a wearable blanket inside. My son plays on three sports teams, so I do a lot of sitting outside on bleachers and turf sidelines—and often at night, when it’s freezing. I’ve tried many things to keep warm, from heated jackets to HotHands, but nothing has worked as well as this water-resistant blanket, which unfurls to 50 x 70 inches and sports a clip at the front so you can wear it like a cape. It can also be used for picnics or as a spot for younger siblings to sit and read during tournaments. It’s also not hard to fold it back up and fit it inside the seat part (which is 1 inch thick without the blanket inside). It comes in six colors, so you can be sure to find one that matches your giftee’s kid’s team or school colors. —Kat Merck.

Industry observers note that as a mom, I take a lot of photos of my family. A lot. And sometimes it feels like all those great photos of my son's milestones go to my camera roll and photo storage to die. There are two solutions I love for this that are incredibly giftable: a digital photo frame she can instantly upload images to, and a printed photo book where you can take the best of the best and put them at her fingertips. I have and love both for different reasons.

I love the digital photo frame to add all the photos from a fun weekend at the San Diego Zoo or Renaissance Pleasure Faire for me to relive again and again, but I also love being able to pull a photo book from the bookshelf and relive a specific moment I know is waiting there for me. Aura makes my favorite digital photo frames (followed by Skylight's Calendar 2 if you want a multipurpose device, but Aura has no subscription fee if you only want photos), while Mixbook has been a favorite of mine for a while when it comes to printing photos, and has great starting prices for its photo books.

In a recent development, the graduation from diaper-bag-carrying mom to tote-full-of-snacks-and-clothes-changes mom to an adult who only needs to carry their own stuff is a parenting milestone that deserves celebration. This is my favorite grown-up mom bag, which holds only the essentials: water (because no matter how old your kids are, someone is going to get thirsty), cards, phone, and keys. The thick strap makes it comfortable to carry, and there’s a color, material, or theme for just about anyone’s vibe, including a new line of clear stadium versions. All WanderFull bags will hold any handle-less water bottle up to 11 inches tall and 3.5 inches in diameter. —Kat Merck.

It has been revealed that once my kiddo is asleep, you can find me parked on the couch playing video games. I upgraded to a Nintendo Switch 2 ($499) earlier this summer so I could finally buy and play Pokopia ($70), since it's exclusive to the new console, and now my husband and I are completely hooked on the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time ($60) remake that came out a few weeks ago. It's also quickly become an experience I can share with my son now that he's 4; he was been helping me and my husband replay Tears of the Kingdom, but now he's dubbed Ocarina of Time as “Massive Little Link” and is obsessed with using the grappling hook and using up all of our arrows.

It has been revealed that if you're not looking to upgrade her console just yet but need a Switch-friendly cozy game for her, Stardew Valley has another substantial patch in the works and only costs $15. I'm also hoping we see Fields of Mistria ($14) come to the Switch eventually, but the full launch came out in August for Steam customers and has major quality-of-life improvements if she has played Stardew one time too many. My husband also upgraded his gaming setup this summer with a Steam Machine (from $1,049), and I have big plans to start using it often for Fields of Mistria. If your mom loves games, she'll love any one of these new devices or new games, especially if she already got herself the new gadget as I did.

Recent findings suggest that if a mom in your life is exploring her nonalcoholic drink options, The Zero Proof has some gift sets perfect to give so she can try out several things at once. I'm right now grounded from drinking any cocktails while I'm pregnant, but moms (and people in general) can have all kinds of reasons to want to explore unique, interesting drinks that are sans alcohol. I really liked this set for how many cool drinks it exposed me to, from bottles of nonalcoholic wine to knockoff cocktails. If you're looking to spend a little less, my favorites so far have been the Château del Ish Non-Alcoholic Sparkling Espumante ($20) and Lapo's Non-Alcoholic Melograno Mule ($20 for four).

According to recent reports, look, I love a Kindle, but if you want to get the best e-reader for your buck (or maybe she just wants an e-reader that isn't a Kindle), the answer is actually a Kobo. My favorite is the Kobo Libra Colour. It's cheaper than the Kindle Colorsoft and can also double as a digital notebook if you add on the $70 stylus. I also prefer Kobo's annotating options: You can write right on the pages instead of in weird pop-up margins and boxes only on Kindle. Kobo also has a page-turner remote ($34), which I love to pair with a pillow stand holder so I can lean back and relax without holding up my e-reader while I read. I gave a similar pillow stand to my mom, and now I can spot her last reading spot easily because that pillow is resting there.

Sources indicate that you could also gift her one of the new Kindles if she's a Kindle addict. Many of my friends are drooling over the new purple Ube color of the 12th-gen Kindle ($150), but my personal favorite is the Kindle Aluminum (I just wish it were cheaper!). There's also finally Kindle page-turn remote, the Kindle Click ($35).

If the mom you know is into LED red-light therapy, she probably already knows about face masks and hair growth devices like the one we recommend above, but there’s one area she’s probably neglecting: her hands. With aging comes loss of collagen, subcutaneous fat, and cumulative effects of UV exposure. I spent the first 26 years of my life living in California, where I rarely remembered to put sunscreen on the tops of my hands. Twenty years later, it demonstrates—they’re wrinkly and have age spots and look like they belong to someone 15 years my senior. Trust me; no mom wants this. I’ve been using Omnilux’s FDA-cleared red-light glove for the past few months to try to mitigate some of the damage, and while I haven’t seen any changes yet (Omnilux indicates changes happen in four to six weeks, but in my experience with red-light masks, it typically takes much longer to see results), I very much enjoy using this device on its own. The soft silicone glove is comfortable to wear and warms as it heats up, so it feels good and works to reduce joint pain. It’s easy to do while I’m reading or watching TV—just three 10-minute sessions per week—and the rechargeable battery (USB-C) lasts a little over a week. If your giftee already spends 10 minutes at the end of the day relaxing in an LED face mask, she’ll know exactly what to do here. —Kat Merck.

In a recent development, if you know a mom who loves to bird-watch (I know one!), you can upgrade her bird feeder to a smart one. Smart bird feeders add a camera to the feeder so she can see a close-up feed of the birds that come to hang out in her yard, and they're adorable to boot, for a little smart curb appeal. WIRED reviewer Kat Merck recommends the original Birdfy feeder as a great gift; it's her favorite smart bird feeder and comes in adorable colors to brighten your mom's yard and catch the eye of neighborhood birds. But the one she and I both have our eye on (her for her mother, me for myself) is the Birdfy Nest Duo, which is actually a birdhouse with two cameras so you can see the birds entering the nest outside and raising a family inside.

I love a backpack when I'm on the move with my 4-year-old, but one thing that annoys me is that things are hard to find inside, because packs are typically so deep. That's why I adore the Mina Baie Emmy Diaper Bag: It's a wide, shallow bag instead of a long one, making it easy to open and see most of what I store in it without digging around. I'm not toting diapers at the moment, but I've used it to pack a ton of snacks, toys, and spare clothing for my kid.

I'm intrigued to see how using it with two kids goes—I chose the Emmy Midi, which is the midsize bag, but if you're a pumping parent or need to carry a ton of bottles with formula, you might want to try the larger Emmy Full. The stylish bag is made of vegan leather and can be converted from crossbody to tote to backpack mode, depending on which straps you use. Mina Baie doesn't include a changing kit, but sells one separately ($59) if you'd like to include it in your gift (or buy that as the gift to upgrade their existing bag of choice).

If Mom loves entertaining—or just being festive—but doesn’t want to have to store a million different dishes, Nora Fleming’s modular serving-tray system is for her. First, pick a base—there are trays, baking dishes, utensil crocks, and even salt and pepper shakers. Then, pick one of dozens of hand-painted “Minis,” or ceramic accents (sold separately). There are holiday themes, sports team themes, and even ones for specific events like mah-jongg or BBQs.

Industry observers note that each base has a hole into which you can attach the Mini with a little rubber stopper. I tested the cracker tray with a harvest-themed Mini, and you wouldn’t know the tray didn’t come with the accent already attached. At the end of next month, I plan to swap it out for a Christmas tree Mini, and so on. Best part is that if Mom likes this setup, you’ll be set on gifts for the foreseeable future, provided you can keep finding new Minis you think she’ll like. —Kat Merck.

It has been revealed that I'm expecting again, and this time I'm on a mission to find a good pregnancy pillow. I tried a large body pillow on the advice of another site for my first pregnancy, and it was honestly an awful experience—the pillow was too large and firm for me to comfortably use, let alone have room for both it and my growing midsection in my bed. Plus, it was heavy, which is annoying when your body already feels too cumbersome to move around.

In a recent development, so far, using the Wildbird Pregnancy Pillow has been the opposite. It's slim and light with just enough squish to add a little support under or around my belly without being difficult to get comfortable. It’s beautiful and easy to maneuver around. Wildbird also suggests it for other support positions postpartum, and I'm curious if those will work for me. But it makes for a beautiful gift for any expecting mom and will be one she's excited to put on her bed and curl up with at night.

For most moms, showers are sacred—especially for moms of babies or younger kids. However, heavy metals, sediments, chlorine, and PFAS can cause health problems not just in drinking water but in water that touches the skin, as well. They can also cause buildup on hair and shower surfaces, making them harder to clean. Many municipalities—including mine—treat water with chlorine, and when I asked him which filter he'd recommend for my own shower, former WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage suggested the Weddell Duo. It's the only US filter he's found that has certification for chlorine and lead removal from NSF International, and it also cites third-party testing by IAPMO R&T showing it can remove PFAS, though there's no corresponding certification.

Still, the Duo has a 2.5-gallon-per-minute flow rate and can remove most chlorine from over 8,000 gallons' worth of showers. It's an in-line filter, so it's easy to install in minutes—just screw it in between your pipe and showerhead. It even comes with a little roll of waterproof tape to ensure a leak-free fit, and because of the horizontal orientation, installation won't affect the showerhead height. The filter needs to be replaced every three months, but refills only run about $25 each, compared with competitors like Filterbaby or Rorra, which can cost $40 to $45. —Kat Merck.

fal Co-Founders Burkay Gur and Gorkem Yurtseven.

Humans are visual creatures. Images and video are the most immersive forms of content. Itâs no accident that more than 80% of internet traffic is video, that social platforms are becoming image- and video-first, and that video games and movies are the largest categories of consumer spend.

In a recent development, generative media will be even bigger. At Sequoiaâs inaugural AI Ascent event in 2023, Jensen Huang made the provocative prediction that âEvery pixel will be generated, not rendered.â Today, that dream appears closer than ever: frontier video and image models have crossed the uncanny valley, and the first compelling use cases of generative media are starting to emerge across advertising, cinema, storytelling and more.

Projects that once demanded years of work and $100M budgets can now be explored much more swiftly and affordably, opening the door to new creative possibilities. Weâre seeing generative media begin to transform familiar media use cases: digital ads, viral TikToks, short films, and micro dramas. There will also be wholly new experiences created that we canât even begin to imagine, from education to personalized media to generated games. The doors to building with creative AI are wide open to anybody with a computer.

fal has built the leading platform for enterprises and developers to build with generative media models. Video models are compute-intensive and finicky to work with, and creating wonderful outputs requires excellence on multiple levels. fal offers AI creatives exactly what they want for this exciting but strange new paradigm, including 400+ models available on-demand across open- and closed-weight (including models like OpenAI Sora and DeepMind Veo), Day 0 support for new model releases, incredibly fast inference speeds, an ergonomic developer API, an advanced playground UI, and enterprise features around model fine-tunes, styles and collaboration.

It has been revealed that falâs customers are the tastemakers of generative media, with use cases ranging from e-commerce (Shopify) to creative suites (Adobe and Canva) to AI-native platforms (Perplexity) to millions of individual developers. While the momentum behind the business has been staggering, we are even more excited by the quality and caliber of teams currently experimenting on fal, creating immersive new education experiences, virtual pets, indie animation studios, and more. If even a small subset of these explorations make it to production, the world will be a dramatically more colorful, entertaining place.

Recent findings suggest that we are delighted to partner with co-founders Burkay Gur (Coinbase ML) and Gorkem Yurtseven (Amazon) and Head of Engineering Batuhan Taskaya (the youngest-ever Python core developer and maintainer). The team is spiky up and down the platform stack, from having one of the best kernel and compiler inference teams in the world, to nurturing model provider relationships with finesse, to grassroots devrel. Their early bet on generative media reveals up across their relationships with model providers, infrastructure performance and ability to dream with creators.

We are at the beginning of a compute explosion in generative video. As the generative media wave accelerates, fal is the inference platform powering the future of AI-first creativity. The team is growing fast to keep up with that demand, and we at Sequoia are proud to lead their Series D.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jake, Alex and their team are giving IT teams the power to bring AI automation from their own department to every part of the organization.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jake, Alex and their team are giving IT teams the power to bring AI automation from their own department to every part of the organization.

Jake, Alex and their team are giving IT teams the power to bring AI automation from their own department to every part of the organization.

IT is one of the most critical functions inside any manufacturer. Every employee depends on it, every system flows through it, and almost every operational challenge eventually becomes an IT problem. When IT slows down, everyone feels it: employees are blocked waiting on support, onboarding is painful, rolling out newly introduced tools gets bottlenecked, and entire company initiatives end up stalled.

Yet despite ITâs central role, the last decade of tooling has not truly empowered them. The powerful tools are heavy to set up and brittle to maintain; the easy-to-use tools focus on narrow use cases and deflection rather than true automation. IT teams are eager to automate and are more technical than business owners. They have experimented with scripts, workflow builders, and more, but the limitations of all these tools still force them to spend the majority of their time on manual work, preventing them from focusing on higher-impact work and enabling the rest of their organizations.

Jake and Alex, the co-founders of Serval, experienced this firsthand at Verkada, where they led Product and Engineering and sold primarily to IT teams. They heard the same half-joking request countless times, and it wasnât about Verkadaâs products. They would ask customers, âWhat else can we build for you?â and IT leaders would reply, âCan you fix my helpdesk too?â These conversations led them to two key insights:.

The first was that true automation only works if it is faster to automate something forever than to do it manually once.

The second came from watching the few IT leaders who did take the time to build automations. They would first describe the workflow in one simple sentence, then reveal a sprawling tree of branches, nodes, conditions, and edge cases. Jake and Alex wondered: what if you could actually build the entire automation the same way you describe it? What if one simple sentence truly was enough?

Sources indicate that these insights were not possible to execute on in the past. Prior generations of AI were not strong enough to make it work, which meant IT teams continued working through manual tasks. That has now changed. With modern LLMs, code generation, and reasoning capabilities, it is finally possible to build a platform where âautomate foreverâ is faster than âfix once.â.

Recent findings suggest that serval is built precisely to deliver on this, and the team is not stopping there. They are using this moment not only to build a system of automation, but to rethink the entire ITSM system of record. As our own Sequoia IT leader, Leon, shared when they chose to become a Serval customer: âServal is not AI for ITSM â it is ITSM built from AI.â.

At the heart of the platform is an AI automation engine that lets teams go from a simple sentence to a deployment-ready automation. IT can describe workflows in natural language, then refine them further â either in natural language or all the way down to code when needed. This combination of being simple enough for anyone to use, yet deep enough for the most advanced IT builders, has resonated strongly with customers. The workflows are fully explainable and traceable, with all necessary permissions included, giving IT teams complete visibility and control and eliminating hallucination risk.

Sources indicate that while their automation engine integrates with existing systems of records, Serval has also built a full-fledged ITSM platform, including a ticketing system, an access management product, an asset management solution, and more. Serval is both the system of engagement and the system of record. This gives IT a single place to build and orchestrate automations, enforce security and compliance, and capture the data that compounds their automation over time.

Sources indicate that customer feedback has been exceptional. We consistently heard how easy Serval is to use, yet how powerful, traceable, and trustworthy its automations are in practice. IT leaders described day-to-day operations being transformed â automation percentages rising every week, employee satisfaction increasing, and IT teams finally having the bandwidth to tackle projects that had been stuck on the back burner for years.

What was also exceptional, and, to be perfectly honest, not something we expected to hear at this stage:.

Many customers have already fully ripped and replaced incumbent ITSM tools and now use Serval as their system of record.

Automation swiftly spread beyond IT into HR, Finance, Legal, Engineering, Security, and more. In some cases, companies have churned off dedicated software vendors for some departments because they rebuilt their workflows directly in Serval.

At Sequoia, the last time we heard such customer feedback that supports the thesis of IT system of record empowering horizontal enterprise automation was 16 years ago, when we partnered with ServiceNow. That is why we were so eager to partner with Serval and preempt their Series B round.

Sources indicate that the market thesis is one half of the story. The other half is the team. References for Jake and Alex â from managers, direct reports, and peers â were glowing. Even more importantly, those references aligned perfectly with the evidence we heard from customers and what weâve observed in talent flows. Strong talent from R&D to GTM is choosing to join Serval, whether or not they have worked with the founders before. The talent density and âpotential energyâ forming around the organization are impressive and represent one of the strongest leading indicators we look for.

Empowering IT teams is an elegant and scalable way to bring AI automation to the enterprise. We are excited to partner with Jake, Alex, and the team at Serval on this journey.

By Anas Biad, Brian Halligan and Alfred Lin.

#26089. 8 Best Travel Adapters (2026): 20+ Models Tested

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

8 Best Travel Adapters (2026): 20+ Models Tested

📅 27 Jul 2021 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3852 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, whether planning a country-hopping odyssey or a quick business trip, your journey will go more smoothly with the best travel adapters that allow you to safely charge all your gadgets wherever you land.
  • The best adapters make great gifts for travelers and deserve a place in your carry-on, but check out our other travel guides, like the Best Travel Essentials, Best Travel Tech for Families, Best Travel Pillows, and Best USB-C Cables.
  • Updated November 2026: I added a Mukiya travel charger and a Mophie Travel Kit, removed some discontinued devices, and updated links and prices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, whether planning a country-hopping odyssey or a quick business trip, your journey will go more smoothly with the best travel adapters that allow you to safely charge all your gadgets wherever you land. After many work trips and family vacations I’ve tested several—both universal and basic options—and my favorites will work in most parts of the world.

The best adapters make great gifts for travelers and deserve a place in your carry-on, but check out our other travel guides, like the Best Travel Essentials, Best Travel Tech for Families, Best Travel Pillows, and Best USB-C Cables.

Updated November 2026: I added a Mukiya travel charger and a Mophie Travel Kit, removed some discontinued devices, and updated links and prices.

There’s a ton to like about this 100-watt universal travel adapter from reliable travel brand Ceptics. It covers more than 200 countries and can charge multiple gadgets in a hurry. The classic slider design pushes out EU, UK, and US plugs, and you can rotate the pins for sockets in Australia and China. I love how securely the plugs lock into place; you must press down firmly to slide them back. You have a universal input socket, an additional side socket for US or Japan plugs, and two USB-C ports and two USB-A ports on the bottom. But what makes this travel adapter my favorite is the retractable USB-C cable. It’s around 25 inches long, the end sticks to the adapter magnetically, and it saves you from having to pack an extra cord. The cable can deliver up to 100 watts in total. The USB-C ports support up to 15 watts, and the USB-A ports go up to 12 watts.

Sources indicate that for all of its strengths, though, it does provide an unfortunate lack of any grounding. Grounding is meant to reduce the risk of an electric shock if there’s a fault, such as a loose wire inside a device with a metal case. (This video explains grounding well.) Thankfully, there’s overload protection with a 10-amp fuse, and it also comes with a spare. But you should not use this adapter with any device with a third metal ground pin on its plug.

I also tested the 140-watt Ceptics 6-in-1 model ($51), which omits the cable but has three USB-C ports and one USB-A, and the excellent 70-watt model ($40), which has the retractable cable but fewer ports and loses the extra outlet. Both are great alternatives.

Perhaps the smallest travel adapter that's still practical to use, the Epicka Air measures 3.46 x 1.97 inches and is just 1.19 inches thick, with the prongs folded away. It’s easy to pack but still feels reasonably sturdy in use. You get one USB-A and three USB-C ports. The first three ports offer up to 15 watts apiece, and the last USB-C port on the right can go up to 65 watts. But 65 watts is also the maximum output across the four ports, so it gets divided if you plug in multiple devices. But if you use the AC outlet too, and you can charge up to five devices at once.

According to recent reports, when I first tested the 40-watt version ($25), I wasn’t sure about this travel adapter, but after using the 65-watt model for a while, I’ve grown to like it. I still think this style of folding design can be a bit fiddly to use, and the prongs sometimes fold back if you bump them while plugging in. But the placement of the EU prongs in the middle helps it stay plugged in more reliably than some larger sliding cube adapters; the US prongs lock into place, and I didn’t have any issues with the UK prongs.

This budget Ceptics device proves that you don’t need to spend that much money to snag one of the best travel adapters. It covers more than 150 countries, with sliders you push to reveal the three most common international plugs—EU, UK, and US. You can rotate the pins for sockets in Australia or China. The sliders lock into place securely, and there’s a button on the side for retracting them. This plug’s universal outlet can recharge your power-hungry devices, like laptops and camera batteries. Two USB-C and two USB-A ports on the bottom, plus a USB-C port on the side, can handle phones, tablets, smartwatches, and Kindles. Each USB-C port can deliver up to 15 watts, and each USB-A port up to 12 watts. While it's not as fast as some of my picks above, you won't care if you tend to charge your gadgets overnight.

There’s no grounding, so don’t plug devices with a third metal ground pin into this adapter. There is an 8-amp fuse for safety, and it comes with a spare. It is also certified by RoHS and CE.

Industry observers note that what I love about this sturdy, compact plug adapter is the lack of sliding pins or moving parts to worry about. It stays put in the outlet. Offered in several versions (Type C, Type E/F, Type G), this adapter enables you to charge up to six gadgets. I’ve been testing the Type G model in Scotland, and it plugs into a single outlet, giving you three US outlets, a USB-A port, and two USB-C ports. The USB-C can output up to 15 watts, and the USB-A ports are limited to 12 watts—not especially speedy, but fine for overnight charging. The adapter is grounded and has various safety features.

According to recent reports, on the downside, it can be tough to use all the outlets simultaneously, as larger plugs, like the MacBook power adapter, tend to block one of the other US outlets. It does not offer surge protection, and the Type G adapter maxes out at 3,250 watts (250 volts, 13 amps), while the EU and other versions top out at 2,500 watts.

If you only need USB-C and USB-A ports for charging your mobile gadgets on the go (and no outlet), I recommend this clever, compact travel adapter. I’ve never seen a mechanism like this before, where you twist to extend the prongs. It's a neat feature. The standard US prongs can be angled for Australia, and there are EU and UK prongs (types A, C, G, and I). The USB-C ports can deliver up to 70 watts, enough to charge a laptop (slowly), and there’s a USB-A port. You could charge up to three devices at once, though the wattage is divided between them, and it got a little warm when I did this. It uses gallium nitride (GaN) technology to keep the size down. This is a new brand to me, but I’ve been testing it on various devices for the last two weeks, and so far, so good.

It has been revealed that universal adapters don't always work properly everywhere, and most don’t have grounding. The cheaper and more reliable alternative is to buy individual adapters. The 12-piece international set from Ceptics is my favorite. It includes types to cover most of the globe, and each is properly grounded. Only visiting a single destination? Just pack the relevant type. These adapters don't have USB ports, so you’ll need the respective charging adapter for your gadgets.

This set is especially good for Europe because it includes Type C, E/F, and G adapters, so you’re covered for any socket. Ceptics offers an even cheaper and smaller five-piece set, but I don’t recommend it. The adapters are flimsy, there’s no grounding, and the European plug’s design doesn’t work well with the recessed sockets you will sometimes encounter. The drawback of plug adapters is that they’re easy to lose, but at least Ceptics includes a small bag for storage.

According to recent reports, this kit includes multiple plug attachments that slide and lock into place to keep you powered across most of the world. It is bulky and much bigger than the average adapter but provides two grounded US AC outlets. There is also a built-in USB-C cable, two USB-A ports, and two USB-C ports. The USB-A ports and built-in USB-C cable offer a combined maximum charging rate of 15 watts. The USB-C ports support Power Delivery, with up to 20 watts each. The top charging rate for all of them simultaneously is 55 watts.

It has been revealed that there is built-in surge protection, but since this is not a voltage converter, don’t plug in hair dryers or other non-dual-voltage electronics. While the two AC outlets are handy, their proximity means that the shape and size of some plugs can make it tricky to use both simultaneously. But with the ability to charge up to seven devices, this kit is handy. I also like the original Ceptics World Travel Adapter Kit ($35), though it lacks the two USB-C ports.

Recent findings suggest that this cute kit comes in a zippered pouch and includes everything you need for a trip. There’s a fold-out charger with a tiltable magnetic Qi2 25W pad for your iPhone or Qi2 Android phone, a 7.5W pad for an Apple Watch, and a 5W pad behind for wireless earbuds. It also includes a 40W power adapter with switchable plugs for the US, UK, EU, and AU—plus a 5-foot USB-C cable. Everything inside comes in color-matched black or cream, unless you opt for the bolder orange-and-teal special edition.

It’s not the most compact option, but I love that everything slots neatly into the included pouch. You can find some great alternatives in my Best Apple 3-in-1 Travel Chargers guide.

What Type of Adapter Do You Need?

It has been revealed that there are 15 plug types in use across the world. Universal adapters tend to cover all of these types.

In a recent development, some countries are not usually covered by universal adapters, such as India (Type D), Israel (Type H), and South Africa (Type M or N). You'll need to buy specific plug adapters for those places. To avoid any surprises when you land, double-check what type you need before you travel.

If you're visiting just one destination, a basic plug adapter that caters to one plug type is all you need. For trips to multiple destinations or for frequent flyers, a universal travel adapter can prove more versatile. The universal adapters I recommend here have the bonus of including multiple USB ports for charging several mobile devices from a single outlet.

Do You Really Need a Voltage Converter?

Voltage converters are major, heavy, and expensive, and they don’t always work—so it’s probably best to avoid them. The reason you might think you need one is that the AC sockets on all of our recommended travel adapters do not convert the voltage coming from the socket. This means plugging into a UK socket will deliver 220 volts at 50 hertz, which is very different from the 120 volts at 60 hertz you can expect in the US. Don't worry! Your gear won’t get fried. You just need to make sure anything you plug into one of these universal travel adapters has something like this printed on it:.

Sources indicate that that should include most modern gadgets. If your device or charger can’t handle a variable voltage, it’s probably best to leave it at home. Most places provide hair dryers, irons, and kettles, so there’s no need to take them with you. It’s also often cheaper to buy a set with the correct plug at your destination and save the luggage space and hassle.

If you are determined to try a voltage converter (again, I don’t recommend doing so), the Ceptics 2,000-watt Travel Voltage Converter ($70) seems to work well. It has a special 2,000-watt outlet for hair dryers, but only ones that work via a mechanical switch (anything with an electronic circuit board for automatic switch-off or temperature control won’t work and is at risk of being fried if plugged in). It also has two outlets that go up to 200 watts, one USB-C port, and three USB-A ports, though the ports do not support fast charging.

Travel adapters and chargers usually state the wattage they can deliver for USB-C and USB-A ports, retractable cables, and wireless charging. If you're interested in getting the fastest rates possible, you’ll want a charger and cable that can deliver the maximum wattage to your device. A laptop might want 100 watts, while a phone only needs 30 watts. There's no need to worry if the charger can deliver more wattage than is required because the device will dictate how much power to draw. If the wattage is lower than required, most devices will simply charge slowly. You can find out more about charging standards like Power Delivery (PD), Quick Charge (QC), and others in my guide on how to fast charge your phone.

Can Travel Adapters Go in a Suitcase?

Yes, you can pack travel adapters in your suitcase. It may be wise to bring one in your hand luggage for easy access should you need to charge up a device when you arrive at your destination. In fact, devices like power banks with lithium batteries (must be capped at 27,000 mAh) must go in hand luggage, not checked bags.

Can I Buy Travel Adapters at the Airport or Hotel?

You certainly can buy travel adapters at the airport, but like all other goods you buy at kiosks between connecting flights, they will be far more expensive than necessary, and your choice will be limited.

According to recent reports, some hotels have travel adapters, and some even have wall outlets for other countries (or USB-A and USB-C ports), but most do not, so don’t bank on it. You can always check with your hotel or accommodation before you depart, but it’s safer to bring a travel adapter with you.

Should You Test Your Travel Adapter Before You Go?

Seriously, nothing is worse than thinking you’re being very clever by packing light only to get to your hotel and discover that your gadgets refuse to charge. Between the adapter, cable, and your device, plenty can go wrong, so do a quick test on your wall outlet at home with everything you are taking before you set off on an international trip.

Anytime I fly for work or vacation, I take a few travel adapters and chargers with me to test. I also test them for longer periods at home in the UK. I have power stations and power strips with US and EU outlets to test those plugs. I test each charger with a variety of devices (iPhone, Pixel, iPad, MacBook, AirPods). I try charging with every port and outlet simultaneously to see if the charger gets warm. I assess the charging rates, durability, size, weight, and usability of each device. If there are any special features, I test them too.

There is an endless amount of travel adapters out there you could buy. While I wholeheartedly recommend one of the options above, there are some other travel adapters I've tested that just barely miss the mark.

Epicka Pulse for $30: The beveled edges of this travel adapter from Epicka make it more comfortable to hold. The sliders work well and lock in place securely to cover you in around 200 countries. A pair of USB-C and two USB-A ports provide a good mix of port options. This adapter can deliver up to 45 watts from either USB-C port, while the USB-A ports top out at 18 watts. I also tested the newer Epicka Pulse Duo ($130), which can deliver up to 140 watts across three USB-C and one USB-A ports, has an extra US or Japanese socket in the side and boasts a smart display that reveals you the current charging status, wattage, and temperature. Cool as it is, it's overkill for most folks and kinda pricey.

Recent findings suggest that tessan Travel Adapter 009 for $20: This is a similar design to the Epicka Air I recommend above, but the prongs don’t stay in place as securely when unfolded, and you can only draw a maximum of 20 watts from the one USB-A and two USB-C ports. But it is affordable and compact. Tessan also makes good, traditional, slider universal adapters: There's a 140-watt model ($70), and the most powerful travel adapter I’ve tested, the Voyager 205 ($128), which has six USB-C ports and one USB-A to deliver up to 205 watts. If you don’t care about charging speed, Tessan's 20W model ($23) is very reasonably priced and offers two USB-A and two USB-C ports in a small package.

It has been revealed that UGreen Travel Plug Adapter for £17: This travel adapter is for UK folks visiting Europe, and it’s a solid option with a fixed plug (no mechanism). It has only two USB-A and one USB-C port for smaller devices, and it’s very bulky. I prefer the OneBeat above for this type of design.

In a recent development, statik SmartCharge Pro for $80: This is a nice combo device that includes a 15,000 mAh power bank and a 60-watt wall charger. There are fold-out US prongs and slide-on adapters for the UK, EU, and AU. You also get one USB-A port, one USB-C port, a fold-out USB-C cable, and a wireless charging pad on top that works with your iPhone or Apple Watch.

D-Link 65W Multi-Port GaN Charger (DCP-651) for $30: If two USB-C ports and a USB-A port are enough for your travel needs, this affordable D-Link charger could be for you. It comes with interchangeable plugs for different countries. The 65-watt limit is enough for overnight charging a laptop and a couple of smartphones.

In a recent development, arsmel VisaPro All-in-One Travel Adapter for $80: This chunky power adapter can charge laptops or multiple small devices with a whopping 170-watt maximum output. It works with any outlet in the US, UK, or EU, thanks to sliding plugs that slot in securely, and you can spin the prongs on the US plug to support the total number of countries (more than 200). I love the mecha-inspired paint job, too. There are four ports along the bottom: two USB-C ports rated at 140 watts, with the third USB-C and USB-A ports rated at 18 watts. It supports PD 3.1, QC 3.0, PPS, FCP, and SCP, and has a 10-amp fuse.

Satechi GaN Travel Charger for $120: If you only take small gadgets with you when you travel, a compact, multi-port wall charger is all you need and a great way to pack light. It plugs directly into the wall and comes with four interchangeable travel adapters for the EU, UK, and Australia, plus a mesh bag to store them. There are four USB-C ports that you can plug your gadgets into, including laptops like the MacBook Pro, tablets, phones, and wearables. With support for Power Delivery 3.1, the first two ports can supply up to 140 watts, and the bottom two ports up to 45 watts. However, the maximum output when all four ports are in use is 145 watts.

Industry observers note that baseus 70W Universal Travel Adapter With Retractable Cable for $40: This excellent travel adapter is almost identical to our top pick from Ceptics, offering up to 70 watts, sliding prongs to cover more than 200 countries, and a built-in retractable USB-C cable, not to mention a USB-C port and two USB-A ports. It also has a snazzy black-and-yellow finish. It only misses out because it’s slightly more expensive, but if you can snag one on sale or prefer the colors, it’s a solid option.

In a recent development, epicka Universal Travel Adapter for $20: This travel adapter from Epicka is still a solid option. The sliding plugs cover 150 countries, and there are four USB-A ports on the bottom and a 15-watt USB-C port on the side. There’s also an 8-amp fuse with a spare, and this adapter is RoHS-, CE-, and FCC-certified.

Recent findings suggest that masterplug Visitor to UK Travel Adapter (3 Pack) for £12: For visitors to the UK, this simple trio of adapters accepts European, American, Australian, and Asian plugs. They are single-outlet adapters with 13-amp fuses inside, and they work perfectly. These are the adapters I use for long-term testing of devices from the US and elsewhere that lack UK plugs. If you forgot to buy an adapter before arriving in the UK, you can find this affordable three-pack at any Argos store.

Industry observers note that anker European Travel Plug Adapter for $16: One of our favorite portable charger brands, Anker, also makes travel adapters. This one plugs into most European outlets to provide a single grounded US outlet, a USB-A port, and two USB-C ports. Unfortunately, the three USB ports max out at 15 watts total, so it’s best for overnight gadget charging, but I appreciate the temperature and overload protection. There is also a UK version ($16).

Industry observers note that epicka Hybrid European Travel Plug Adapter for $26: This handy adapter turns one outlet into four and includes four USB ports (two A and two C). It has fold-out Type A prongs, but you can also slide on a fold-out Type C plug for use in Europe. While the USB ports support QC 3.0 or PD 3.0, they max out at 20 watts in total. I prefer the OneBeat adapters recommended above.

You can do better than these travel adapters.

In a recent development, EZQuest WorldTravel GaN 5 Port With PD Wall Charger: This travel adapter has a generous four USB-C ports and one USB-A port with a familiar slide-out prong design that covers more than 150 countries. There’s also a built-in 10-amp fuse and a spare. It has RoHS, CE, and FCC certification. It works fine, but it's kinda boxy, and the sliders don't lock in place as securely as some of our other picks. There's also a 65W version ($60).

Rolling Square Pocket Travel Adapter: I admire any attempt to shrink down travel adapters in size, but the three-pronged UK plugs are usually the obstacle. Rolling Square’s solution is to have a flip-out third prong, but you’ll need a good fingernail to unhitch it. This charger has a single USB-C port capable of delivering up to 30 watts and is a compact option that covers the US, UK, and Europe.

Ceptics 65W World Travel Adapter.

Sources indicate that ceptics 65W World Travel Adapter: This versatile adapter comes with Type A, B, C, E/F, G, and I slide-on plugs. They fit onto the rectangular brick and plug directly into the outlet, or you can attach them to the optional five-foot cable. The brick has one grounded US outlet and a second non-grounded outlet, with one USB-A (30-watt) and two USB-C (65- and 33-watt) ports at the other end. It works fine, and it's affordable, but it's bulky and ugly.

According to recent reports, updated November 23: I’ve added new deals on machines from Diletta, Fellow, and De'Longhi, plus some accessories. I've also ensured up-to-date links and prices.

WIRED reviewers have tried and liked a couple of machines from Diletta, a line of Italian-made, classic semiautomatics exclusive to Seattle Coffee Gear, and they’re all on sale today through December 14.

We reviewed the Bello+ in 2024, appreciating the stylish, industrial design (handmade in Milan) and easily maneuverable steam wand. Our reviewer found it a bit finicky, but Seattle Coffee Gear says it does have a programmable pre-infusion for repeatable recipes.

Best Traditional Espresso Machine in our guide to the best, the Mio is stylish and built to last, with an analog design and a two-year warranty. It also makes for a solid first “real” espresso machine with its built-in shot timer and pressure gauge.

Fellow set some pretty lofty expectations with the release of its sleek Aiden coffee maker in 2024, and according to former WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage, the brand didn't disappoint on its first attempt at an espresso machine. The ability to adjust flow rates and pressure curves was once the province of, as Korfhage put it, only the “richest and nerdiest of nerds.” But Fellow now allows you—yes, you, at home in your kitchen—to fine-tune how water moves through the grounds, unlocking previously unforeseen dimensions of flavor.

When we tested this machine, we liked it for a variety of reasons, including an easy-to-use milk frother and two swappable bean hoppers, which are especially helpful if you like to switch to decaf in the afternoons. Sources indicate that this flashy, design-oriented semiautomatic (“a steampunk gasworks of a thing,” according to Korfhage) is quite dramatic in person. Note that this sale is on the 2nd Gen machine, which features expanded grinder settings and a latest portafilter.

According to recent reports, formerly the Linea Classic, De’Longhi’s Classic is the best bare-bones espresso machine we’ve tried, with a pressure gauge, 15-bar pump, and updated thermoblock system. Industry observers note that the Vertuo Pop+ is our favorite pod maker for espresso. The Deluxe model adds a larger, side-mount water tank (37 ounces to the original’s 25 ounces) and new finishes, including this white one, a matte black-and-gold, and a sort of gunmetal gray.

We appreciated this semiautomatic’s slim profile, consistent shots, and built-in burr grinder. Even so, it’s a beautiful, industrial-looking machine that takes up only 12 inches of counter space.

It’s got a built-in grinder and milk frother, the latter of which can make cold foam and even has a setting for plant-based milk. In true Ninja fashion, it also has settings for drip coffee and cold brew, but neither impressed our tester, so I wouldn’t buy it for those features alone.

Former WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage tested Terra Kaffe's newer Demi and said it was perhaps the “dead-simplest fully automatic espresso machine I've yet encountered that still makes good coffee,” with just a dial and a button. Though it didn't come out on top during a blind espresso taste test we did earlier this year, it's still a great-looking machine that's easy to use and is a whopping $400 off (or $500 with a coffee subscription) for Black Friday.

Atlas (6-month Gift subscription).

Former barista and WIRED contributing reviewer Pete Cottell likes this little scale that includes three magnetic add-ons: a platform, a metal dosing cup, and a catch cup that fits directly onto almost any portafilter.

If grounds are sticking to the plastic components of your coffee grinder, Cottell recommends adding this durable, stylish spray bottle to your espresso setup.

Cottell likes situating this mat underneath your espresso setup, as the lip contains spills and the textured portion is great for drying tools post-washing.

Industry observers note that some machines come with a tamper; others don't. If yours doesn’t, Cottell recommends you get this one. The spring-loaded base unloads 15 pounds of force to create a perfectly flat puck inside your portafilter. (A click lets you know when to stop pushing, so it’s great for beginners, too.).

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Saddle up: Your dreams for 2030 just became possible for 2026.

Saddle up: Your dreams for 2030 just became possible for 2026.

Years ago, some leading researchers told us that their objective was AGI. Eager to hear a coherent definition, we naively asked âhow do you define AGI?â. They paused, looked at each other tentatively, and then offered up whatâs since become something of a mantra in the field of AI: âwell, we each kind of have our own definitions, but weâll know it when we see it.â.

Industry observers note that this vignette typifies our quest for a concrete definition of AGI. It has proven elusive.

It has been revealed that while the definition is elusive, the reality is not. AGI is here, now.

Recent findings suggest that coding agents are the first example. There are more on the way.

Long-horizon agents are functionally AGI, and 2026 will be their year.

Before we go any further, itâs worth acknowledging that we do not have the moral authority to propose a technical definition of AGI.

Recent findings suggest that we are investors. We study markets, founders, and the collision thereof: businesses.

Given that, ours is a functional definition, not a technical definition. Latest technical capabilities beg the Don Valentine question: so what?

The answer resides in real world impact.

In a recent development, AGI is the ability to figure things out. Thatâs it.*.

According to recent reports, *We appreciate that such an imprecise definition will not settle any philosophical debates. Pragmatically speaking, what do you want if youâre trying to get something done? An AI that can just figure stuff out. How it happens is of less concern than the fact that it happens.

A human who can figure things out has some baseline knowledge, the ability to reason over that knowledge, and the ability to iterate their way to the answer.

An AI that can figure things out has some baseline knowledge (pre-training), the ability to reason over that knowledge (inference-time compute), and the ability to iterate its way to the answer (long-horizon agents).

Recent findings suggest that the first ingredient (knowledge / pre-training) is what fueled the original ChatGPT moment in 2022. The second (reasoning / inference-time compute) came with the release of o1 in late 2024. The third (iteration / long-horizon agents) came in the last few weeks with Claude Code and other coding agents crossing a capability threshold.

Generally intelligent people can work autonomously for hours at a time, making and fixing their mistakes and figuring out what to do next without being told. Generally intelligent agents can do the same thing. This is latest.

According to recent reports, A founder messages his agent: âI need a developer relations lead. Someone technical enough to earn respect from senior engineers, but who actually enjoys being on Twitter. We sell to platform teams. Go.â.

The agent starts with the obvious: LinkedIn searches for âDeveloper Advocateâ and âDevRelâ at competing companies â Datadog, Temporal, Langchain. It finds hundreds of profiles. But job titles donât reveal whoâs actually good at this.

Sources indicate that it pivots to signal over credentials. It searches YouTube for conference talks. It finds 50+ speakers, then filters for those with talks that have strong engagement.

It cross-references those speakers with Twitter. Half have inactive accounts or just retweet their employerâs blog posts. Not what we want. But a dozen have real followings â they post real opinions, reply to people, and get engagement from developers. And their posts have real taste.

Sources indicate that the agent narrows further. It checks whoâs been posting less frequently in the last three months. A drop in activity sometimes signals disengagement from their current role. Three names surface.

Industry observers note that it researches those three. One just confirmed a new role â too late. One is a founder of a company that just raised funding â not leaving. The third is a senior DevRel at a Series D company that just did layoffs in marketing. Her last talk was about exactly the platform engineering space the startup targets. She has 14k Twitter followers and posts memes that actual engineers engage with. She hasnât updated her LinkedIn in two months.

The agent drafts an email acknowledging her recent talk, the overlap with the startupâs ICP, and a specific note about the creative freedom a smaller team offers. It suggests a casual conversation, not a pitch.

Total time: 31 minutes. The founder has a shortlist of one instead of a JD posted to a job board.

According to recent reports, this is what it means to figure things out. Navigating ambiguity to accomplish a goal â forming hypotheses, testing them, hitting dead ends, and pivoting until something clicks. The agent didnât follow a script. It ran the same loop a great recruiter runs in their head, except it did it tirelessly in 31 minutes, without being told how.

To be clear: agents still fail. They hallucinate, lose context, and sometimes charge confidently down exactly the wrong path. But the trajectory is unmistakable, and the failures are increasingly fixable.

In last yearâs essay, we wrote about reasoning models as the most vital fresh frontier for AI. Long-horizon agents push this paradigm further by allowing models to take actions and iterate over time.

Coaxing a model to think for longer is not trivial. A base reasoning model can think for seconds or minutes.

In a recent development, two different technical approaches seem to both be working and scaling well: reinforcement learning and agent harnesses. The former approach teaches a model intrinsically to stay on track for longer by poking and prodding it to maintain focus during the training process. The latter designs specific scaffolding around the known limitations of models (memory hand-offs, compaction, and more).

Sources indicate that scaling reinforcement learning is the domain of the research labs. They have made exceptional progress on this front, from multi-agent systems to reliable tool use.

Designing great agent harnesses is the domain of the application layer. Some of the most beloved products on the market today are known for their exceptionally engineered agent harnesses: Manus, Claude Code, Factoryâs Droids, etc.

Recent findings suggest that if thereâs one exponential curve to bet on, itâs the performance of long-horizon agents. METR has been meticulously tracking AIâs ability to complete long-horizon tasks. The rate of progress is exponential, doubling every ~7 months. If we trace out the exponential, agents should be able to work reliably to complete tasks that take human experts a full day by 2028, a full year by 2034, and a full century by 2037.

It has been revealed that soon youâll be able to hire an agent. Thatâs one litmus test for AGI (h/t: Sarah Guo).

In a recent development, you can âhireâ GPT-5.2 or Claude or Grok or Gemini today. More examples are on the way:.

Medicine: OpenEvidenceâs Deep Consult functions as a specialist.

Law: Harveyâs agents function as an Associate.

Cybersecurity: XBOW functions as a pen-tester.

DevOps: Traversalâs agents function as an SRE.

GTM: Day AI functions as a BDR, SE, and Rev Ops leader.

Recruiting: Juicebox functions as a recruiter.

Math: Harmonicâs Aristotle functions as a mathematician.

Semiconductor Design: Ricursiveâs agents function as chip designers.

AI Researcher: GPT-5.2 and Claude function as AI researchers.

This has profound implications for founders.

Sources indicate that the AI applications of 2023 and 2024 were talkers. Some were very sophisticated conversationalists! But their impact was limited.

It has been revealed that the AI applications of 2026 and 2027 will be doers. They will feel like colleagues. Usage will go from a few times a day to all-day, every day, with multiple instances running in parallel. People wonât save a few hours here and there â theyâll go from working as an IC to managing a team of agents.

Remember all that talk of selling work? Now itâs possible.

What work can you accomplish? The capabilities of a long-horizon agent are drastically different than a single forward pass of a model. What fresh capabilities do long-horizon agents unlock in your domain? What tasks require persistence, where sustained attention is the bottleneck?

Recent findings suggest that how will you productize that work? How will your application interface evolve in your domain, as the UI of work grows from chatbot to agent delegation?

Can you do that work reliably? Are you obsessively improving your agent harness? Do you have a strong feedback loop?

How can you sell that work?Can you price and package to value and outcomes?

Itâs time to ride the long-horizon agent exponential.

In a recent development, today, your agents can probably work reliably for ~30 minutes. But theyâll be able to perform a dayâs worth of work very soon â and a centuryâs worth of work eventually.

What can you achieve when your aims are measured in centuries? A century is 200,000 clinical trials no oneâs cross-referenced. A century is every customer support ticket ever filed, finally mined for signal. A century is the entire U.S. tax code, refactored for coherence.

The ambitious version of your roadmap just became the realistic one.
