📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The next $1T company will be a software company masquerading as a services firm.
  • Industry observers note that every founder building an AI tool is asking the same question: what happens when the next version of Claude makes my product a feature?
  • It has been revealed that writing code is mostly intelligence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The next $1T company will be a software company masquerading as a services firm.

Industry observers note that every founder building an AI tool is asking the same question: what happens when the next version of Claude makes my product a feature? Theyâre right to worry. If you sell the tool, youâre in a race against the model. But if you sell the work, every improvement in the model makes your service faster, cheaper, and harder to compete with. A manufacturer might spend $10K a year for QuickBooks and $120K on an accountant to close the books. The next legendary company will just close the books.

It has been revealed that writing code is mostly intelligence. Knowing what to build next is judgement.

Translating a spec into code, testing, debugging: the rules are complex but they are rules. Judgement is different. It requires experience and taste, instinct built on years of practice. Deciding which feature to build next, whether to take on tech debt, when to ship before itâs ready.

Recent findings suggest that A year ago, most Cursor people treated AI as autocomplete. Today, more tasks are started by agents than by humans. Software engineering accounts for over half of all AI tool usage across professions. Every other category is still in single digits. The reason is that software engineering is primarily intelligence work. AI has crossed the threshold where it can do most of the intelligence work autonomously and leave the judgement to humans. Software engineering got there first. It is coming to every single profession.

Recent findings suggest that A copilot sells the tool. An autopilot sells the work.

Until recently, AI models were still developing intelligence and judgement, so the right approach was to build a copilot first: put AI in the hands of a professional and let them decide what to do with it. Harvey sells to law firms. Rogo sells to investment banks. The professional is the customer, the tool makes them more productive, and they take responsibility for the output.

Sources indicate that today, the models are intelligent enough that in some categories the best place to start is as an autopilot. Crosby sells to the organization that needs an NDA drafted, not to outside counsel. WithCoverage sells to the CFO who needs insurance, not to the broker. The customer is buying the outcome directly. The work budget in any profession dwarfs the tool budget, and autopilots capture the work budget from day one.

The higher the intelligence ratio in any field, the sooner autopilots will win.

In a recent development, todayâs judgement will become tomorrowâs intelligence. As AI systems accumulate proprietary data about what good judgement looks like in their domain, the frontier will shift. Copilots and autopilots will converge. The copilot-to-autopilot transition has already begun in several categories. But the starting position matters because it determines where autopilots can win customers now and begin compounding the data that will eventually let them handle judgement too.

The Autopilot Playbook: Outsourcing as the Wedge.

For every dollar spent on software, six are spent on services.

The total addressable market for autopilots is all labour spend in a category, insourced and outsourced combined. But the right place to start is where outsourcing already exists.

According to recent reports, if a task is already outsourced, it tells you three things. One, the tech giant has accepted that this work can be done externally. Two, thereâs an existing budget line that can be substituted cleanly. Three, the buyer is already purchasing an outcome. Replacing an outsourcing contract with an AI-native services provider is a vendor swap. Replacing headcount is a reorg.

Industry observers note that the playbook: companies should start with the outsourced, intelligence-heavy task. Nail distribution. Expand toward the insourced, judgement-heavy work as the AI compounds. The outsourced task is the wedge. The insourced work is the long-term TAM.

Industry observers note that crosby started with NDAs: a well-defined task, primarily intelligence, that most companies already outsource to external counsel. The budget exists, the scope is clear, the ROI is immediate, and the substitution is frictionless.

Plotting every services vertical on an intelligence-to-judgement spectrum and outsourced-to-insourced ratio produces a priority map with labour TAM in brackets. The list is illustrative.

Insurance brokerage ($140-200B). The largest dollar market on this list. Standard commercial lines are highly standardised: the brokerâs value-add is essentially shopping across carriers and filling forms, pure intelligence work. The distribution layer is incredibly fragmented, tens of thousands of small brokers each running the same process, so no single incumbent controls the customer relationship. WithCoverage and Harper are interesting newcomers.

Accounting and audit ($50-80B outsourced in the US alone). The US has lost roughly 340,000 accountants over five years while demand has grown. 75% of CPAs are nearing retirement, the licensing path is long, and starting salaries lag tech and finance. That structural shortage is pushing firms to accept AI faster than almost any other profession. Rillet is building the AI-native ERP that will close the books. Basis started as a copilot for accountants.

Healthcare revenue cycle ($50-80B outsourced in US). People hear âhealthcareâ and assume itâs judgement-heavy, but the billing layer is almost pure intelligence. Medical coding is translating clinical notes into ~70,000 standardised ICD-10 codes. The rules are complex but they are rules. The outsourcing is already mature and outcome-based. An autopilot just has to do the same thing at lower cost. Anterior is the furthest along.

Claims adjusting ($50-80B including TPAs). On the other side of the insurance policy, claims adjusting is a separate autopilot surface. Standard-line claims are settled by interpreting policy language against damage schedules and setting reserves using actuarial tables. The adjuster workforce is aging out and nobodyâs replacing them. The market is massively outsourced to independents and TPAs like Crawford and Sedgwick. One industry, at least two distinct autopilot opportunities. Pace is building the autopilot for claims handling. Strala is building an AI-native TPA.

Tax advisory ($30-35B). CPA licensing creates a regulatory moat, but 80-90% of the underlying work is intelligence. Every additional jurisdiction a tax autopilot handles deepens its data moat. Multi-jurisdiction complexity is exactly what SMBs outsource because no single in-house accountant can cover it. TaxGPT is an early mover alongside Skalar and Ravical in Europe.

According to recent reports, legal, transactional work ($20-25B). Contract drafting, NDAs, regulatory filings: high intelligence, routinely outsourced. The work product is standardised enough that quality is verifiable, so the buyer can trust AI output without deep legal expertise. Harvey is the emerging leader and is moving promptly to autopilot; Crosby and Lawhive are the autopilot-native newcomers.

Sources indicate that IT managed services ($100B+). Every SMB outsources its IT. Patching, monitoring, user provisioning, alert triage: intelligence work running on repeat across thousands of identical environments. The existing software layer (ConnectWise, Datto) sells tools to the MSP. Nobody has yet sold âyour IT runsâ directly to the organization as an outcome. Edra is automating IT processes. Serval is automating IT support.

In a recent development, supply chain and procurement ($200B+). Most enterprises negotiate seriously with only their top 20% of suppliers. The long tail gets zero attention because itâs not economical to have humans do the work. Contract leakage runs 2-5% of total procurement spend. The wedge is abandoned work: no budget line to justify, no incumbent to displace, just found money. Magentic is building the AI for direct procurement, AskLio for indirect procurement. Tacto is building both the system of record and copilot for the midmarket.

In a recent development, recruitment and staffing ($200B+). The largest services market on this list. The top of the hiring funnel (screening, matching, outreach) is pure intelligence, but closing a candidate and assessing culture fit is judgement built on years of pattern recognition. The autopilot wedge exists in high-volume, low-judgement roles where matching is standardised. Juicebox, Mercor, Jack & Jill are emerging leaders building across the spectrum.

Management consulting ($300-400B). Huge market but the work is mostly judgement. The interesting question is whether AI can disaggregate consulting into intelligence components (data gathering, benchmarking) and judgement components (strategic recommendations), with the intelligence layer getting automated and the judgement layer staying human. Best candidates TBD.

According to recent reports, in 2025, the fastest-growing AI companies were copilots. In 2026, many will try to become autopilots. They have the product and the customer knowledge. But they also face the innovatorâs dilemma: selling the work means cutting their own customers out of doing it. Thatâs the opening for pure-play autopilots.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yet another former member of the so-called Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) appears to have exited the government only to return as a contractor.

In September, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) put out a call for a contract worth $200,000 for “modernization discovery, prototyping, and implementation-planning engagement.” Four days later, the department closed the bidding process and awarded the contract to Yat Choi LLC, a company owned by a former Airbnb engineer and Canadian citizen named Yat Choi, whose company also goes by the name GovMaxxing.

In a recent development, at the time, Choi had left his role at the National Design Studio (NDS)—the group tasked with redesigning government websites—just a few weeks prior. Before that, Choi worked at DOGE.

It has been revealed that the bid was for a project set to run for a little under six months, and the contract was awarded as sole-source, meaning that it did not go through a normal competitive bidding process. In the documentation announcing the award, HHS justified this decision by saying that its “market research and source rationale found that conventional consulting firms generally would need to assemble a multidisciplinary team or obtain additional technical resources” to provide the required skills around “business-process modernization, artificial intelligence, automation, technical architecture, and rapid prototyping.”.

In October, a organization called CoA Solutions lodged what’s known as a bid protest with the Government Accountability Office (GAO) contesting the agency’s decision to award the contract to Choi. CoA Solutions is a small business that builds AI software for the government and received another contract with the Treasury Department in 2024.

Ari Perez, the CEO of CoA Solutions, tells WIRED that his firm made a bid below the $200,000 award price, and it proposed two experts doing the work full-time, including Perez himself.

Industry observers note that perez says that CoA asked HHS for an explanation of the award on October 8 and, when it did not receive one, filed its protest with the GAO the next day. Perez says that his company’s sole contestation was about how the bids were evaluated by HHS, not about Choi or his work with NDS.

According to recent reports, “I'm a service-disabled veteran. I've served this government since I was 17 at West Point. At the US Digital Service I helped deliver for veterans at the VA, and later I worked on asylum and immigration systems at DHS. I started CoA to keep doing impactful government work,” claims Perez. “We want to win on merit, and if HHS reopens it, we'll bid again.”.

Recent findings suggest that according to CoA, in response to the bid protest, HHS terminated the award to Choi and canceled the call for contractors. With the cancellation, the GAO dismissed the protest without investigating it further. A GAO spokesperson referred WIRED to HHS.

Sources indicate that “HHS remains committed to modernizing its systems to improve efficiency and better serve the American people,” says HHS spokesperson Grace Davis Jamison. “Following a bid protest challenging the award, HHS voluntarily took corrective action, terminating the contract at no cost to the government and canceling the solicitation.”.

Sources indicate that choi’s role in the US government has not been exactly clear. In his bio on X, Choi writes that he was part of both DOGE and NDS, and noted in a post that he was recruited by billionaire Elon Musk and Joe Gebbia, Airbnb’s cofounder, to help modernize the retirement system at the Office of Personnel Management (OPM). Gebbia now leads NDS, which was created after Musk left government and which has served as a landing pad for several DOGE members, including Edward “Significant Balls” Coristine.

In December 2025, Choi contributed to a blog on the NDS website about automating the federal retirement system. But on his LinkedIn, Choi lists himself as a senior technologist at OPM. On November 5, just two days after Republicans lost the midterm elections, Choi announced in a post on X that he had left OPM and was launching his organization, GovMaxxing, through which he plans to continue to contract with the government. GovMaxxing operates as Yat Choi LLC federally.

In response to questions from WIRED about his role in government, Choi claims that he “was recruited to support federal modernization efforts and subsequently onboarded as an OPM contractor.” There, Choi says, he “contributed to modernization efforts associated with DOGE and subsequently NDS. I was not, and have never been, a federal government employee.” Choi claims he left OPM in mid-August, though OPM did not respond to questions confirming whether this was the case. “I began actively pursuing the contracting opportunity after my engagement with OPM ended,” says Choi.

Industry observers note that choi confirmed that he is a Canadian citizen and a “lawful permanent resident” of the US. Foreigners are not generally allowed to hold full-time roles in government or serve as special government employees. The rules are more flexible for contractors. During the height of DOGE’s activity, a close Musk ally, Baris Akis, was prevented from joining the group as a special government employee because he is a Turkish citizen, according to The Atlantic. Akis, however, continued to serve as a recruiter for the group.

On his website, Choi labels the “client” for his work in government as “US Office of Personnel Management / DOGE / National Design Studio” and describes himself as the “modernization lead.” However, documents indicate that Choi’s tech giant was not registered in the state of New York until April 2026, and in the System for Award Management, the procurement website where US government contractors bid, there are no other contracts for Choi’s work. “None of my work at OPM was performed through my LLC. My website references my prior professional experience at OPM and does not attribute that work to my company,” says Choi.

Choi says that the HHS contract was for a “separate modernization discovery project. It was not a continuation of any work with OPM, DOGE, or NDS.”.

Recent findings suggest that according to the code of federal regulations, except in very specific circumstances, government contracts cannot be awarded to government employees or to organizations they fully or partially own. But Jessica Tillipman, associate dean for government procurement law studies at George Washington University, claims that even though Choi was not a regular government employee, the fact that he was part of DOGE and NDS, whose work has spanned across government agencies, could create the appearance of a conflict of interest with regard to the HHS contract. “The baseline posture of the federal acquisition regulation is to strictly avoid conflicts of interest or even the appearance of them,” says Tillipman. “So agencies all have a duty, and the contracting teams have a duty, to make sure that they are considering these things when they're awarding these contracts.”.

Industry observers note that choi tells WIRED that HHS “initiated contact and expressed interest” in his “modernization experience” before the call for bids was announced. HHS did not respond to questions about whether the bid had been written specifically for him.

Recent findings suggest that tillipman notes that while the government may sometimes create a contracting opportunity designed for a specific person or organization, “it’s generally niche or highly specialized work." Tillipman notes that the fact that there were 75 bids placed on the contract indicates that this is “not a unique service.” She notes that the government’s justification for a sole-source contract is “thin.” “Usually, when there's only one responsible source, there's a technical reason,” she says. This could be something like a special tool that is not interoperable with outside software, or when there is only one company that can provide a specific service or that makes a certain physical part that might be used for weapons or specialized machinery.

According to recent reports, on the GovMaxxing website, Choi notes that potential government clients can work with the manufacturer as a prime contractor or “subcontract through one of our partner primes your agency may already be working with.” Unlike prime contracts, there is no way to publicly see which subcontractor a prime contractor works with. Choi declined to name the companies or current “prime” contractors he subcontracts under.

But Tillipman states that even if Choi were to take on another version of the HHS contract for a subcontractor, similar questions could still be raised within the agency and externally should it ever come to light. “In certain instances, your subcontractors’ conflicts can be imputed to the prime contractor,” she says. “The whole thing is highly irregular overall.”.

According to recent reports, choi is not the only former DOGE or NDS member who appears to be hoping to benefit from federal contracts after leaving the government. Earlier this year, WIRED reported that Ethan Shaotran, one of the young engineers who formed the early core of DOGE, had started a defense tech startup. The startup has been listed on the System for Award Management since April. Former DOGE members Jack Stein, Gavin Kliger, Luke Farritor, and Marko Elez introduced an AI defense technology company called Cathedral, which has been listed on the System for Award Management since July. Neither have received “prime” contracts with any federal agency, but whether they have been taken on as subcontractors to other prime contractors is unclear.

Despite the HHS contract’s cancellation, Choi appears undeterred. Earlier this week, following the nationwide grounding of flights by the Federal Aviation Administration, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called for funding to modernize air traffic control in a post on X. In response, Choi wrote, “Secretary Duffy, I’m the DOGE engineer who led the modernization of federal retirement processing at OPM last year … I’ve since started a organization to work with more agencies, and we’d love to help with the FAA’s modernization efforts. Put us in, coach!”.

The Hatch Baby is now in his room and keeps him asleep each night with its music, while I have the Hatch Restore for myself.

Everyone on TikTok might talk about the MomCozy washer, but the best baby bottle washer WIRED reviewer Nicole Kinning found actually comes from Grownsy. Early parenting is survival, and bandwidth to go to the grocery store or cook becomes a hard zero. There’s a reason friends and family often run food trains for new parents. The following food gifts would be a great option to contribute to a food train, and being shippable packages means you can send them to a friend or family member you may live too far from to visit often.

Shop (The Ultimate Mama + Baby Gift Set).

In a recent development, where has this organizer been in my four years of parenting? In a recent development, if you’re looking to spend a little more on the new parents, these smart home and connected gadgets will genuinely improve their everyday life. Sources indicate that if they’re worried about baby’s temperature at night (I’m permanently haunted by the phrase about warm babies, so much that I won’t type it here), getting a smart thermostat that pairs with a temperature sensor lets you dial in the right climate for baby’s room, separate from the whole house. Sources indicate that any household chore that can be eliminated when adjusting to a new baby is a huge help. If they’re a cat owner but don’t have an automatic litter box, this is our favorite one to help eliminate daily scooping and cleaning.

I’ve changed the lives of multiple parents by hooking them on robot vacuums. A lot of people still think a robot vacuum is a useless machine that gets lost and eats your power cords, but today’s modern models are smart, powerful, precise, and pull double duty as mops. My latest pick is the Qrevo 2 Pro, especially when it’s on sale.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that at Sequoia, we see that speed is the best predictor of start-up success. Most companies are focused on AI as a productivity enhancer. Few are focused on the potential of AI to change how we work together. Block is showing what it looks like to fundamentally rethink organization design, ultimately harnessing AI to increase speed as a compounding competitive advantage.

Two thousand years before the first corporate org chart, the Roman Army solved a problem that every large organization still faces: how do you coordinate thousands of people across vast distances with limited communication?

In a recent development, their answer was a nested hierarchy with a consistent span of control at every level. The smallest unit was the contubernium, eight soldiers who shared a tent, equipment, and a mule, led by a decanus. Ten contubernia formed a century of eighty men under a centurion. Six centuries made a cohort. Ten cohorts made a legion of roughly 5,000. At each layer, a named commander held defined authority, aggregated information from below, and relayed decisions from above. The structure (8 â 80 â 480 â 5,000) was an information routing protocol built around a simple human limitation: a leader can effectively manage somewhere between three and eight people. The Romans discovered this through centuries of warfare. Even today, the US Armyâs hierarchical chain follows a similar pattern. We now call it âspan of control,â and it remains the governing constraint of every large organization on earth.

Industry observers note that the next big change came from Prussia. After Napoleonâs army destroyed the Prussian forces at the Battle of Jena in 1806, a group of reformers led by Scharnhorst and Gneisenau rebuilt the military around an uncomfortable truth: you cannot depend on individual genius at the top. You need a system. They created the General Staff, a dedicated class of trained officers whose job was not to fight but to plan operations, process information, and coordinate across units. Scharnhorst intended these staff officers to âsupport incompetent Generals, providing the talents that might otherwise be wanting among leaders and commanders.â This was middle management before the term existed. Professionals whose purpose was to route information, pre-compute decisions, and maintain alignment across a complex organization. The military also formalized the distinction between âlineâ and âstaffâ functions. Line advances the core mission. Staff provides specialized support. Every corporation still uses this vocabulary today.

Military hierarchy entered the business world through the American railroads in the 1840s and 1850s. The U.S. Army lent West Point-trained engineers to private railroad companies, and these officers brought military organizational thinking with them. Staff and line hierarchies, divisional structure, bureaucratic systems of reporting and control: all of it was developed in the military before the railroads adopted it. In the mid-1850s, Daniel McCallum of the New York and Erie Railroad created the worldâs first organizational chart to manage a system stretching over 500 miles with thousands of workers. The informal management styles that worked for smaller railroads were failing. Train collisions were killing people. McCallumâs chart formalized the same hierarchical logic the Romans had used: layers of authority, defined reporting lines, structured information flow. It became the blueprint for the modern corporation.

Frederick Taylor (1856-1915), often called the âFather of Scientific Management,â optimized what happened within that hierarchy. Taylor broke work into specialized tasks, assigned them to trained experts, and managed through measurement rather than intuition. This produced the functional pyramid organization â a structure optimized for efficiency within the information routing system that the military had pioneered and the railroads had commercialized.

According to recent reports, the first real stress test of functional hierarchy came during World War II. The Manhattan Project required physicists, chemists, engineers, metallurgists, and military officers to work across disciplinary boundaries toward a single objective under extreme secrecy and time pressure. Robert Oppenheimer organized Los Alamos into functional divisions but insisted on open collaboration across them, resisting the militaryâs instinct to compartmentalize. When the implosion problem became critical in 1944, he reorganized the lab around it, creating cross-functional teams unlike anything in corporate America at the time. It worked, but it was a wartime exception led by a singular figure. The question the postwar business world faced was whether that kind of cross-functional coordination could be made routine.

With the growth and globalization of companies after World War II, the scale limitations of functional design became acute. In 1959, McKinseyâs Gilbert Clee and Alfred di Scipio published âCreating a World Enterpriseâ in the Harvard Business Review, providing an intellectual framework for a matrix organization that combined functional specialties with divisional units. Under the leadership of Marvin Bower, McKinsey helped companies like Shell and GE implement these principles, balancing central standards with local agility. This became the âprofessionalâ or âmodernâ corporation that propelled the postwar global economy.

Over time, other frameworks emerged to address the complexity, rigidity, and bureaucracy of matrix structures. The McKinsey 7-S framework, developed in the late 1970s by Tom Peters and Robert Waterman, distinguished the âhard Ssâ (Strategy, Structure, Systems) from the âsoft Ssâ (Shared Values, Skills, Staff, Style). The core idea was that structural elements alone were insufficient. Organizational effectiveness required alignment across cultural traits and the human factors that determine whether a strategy actually succeeds.

According to recent reports, in more recent decades, technology companies have experimented aggressively with organization structure. Spotify popularized cross-functional squads with short sprint cycles. Zappos attempted Holacracy, eliminating management titles entirely. Valve operated with a flat structure and no formal hierarchy. Each of these experiments revealed something about the limitations of traditional hierarchy, but none solved the underlying problem. Spotify moved back toward conventional management as it scaled. Zappos saw significant attrition. Valveâs model proved difficult to scale beyond a few hundred people. As organizations grow into the thousands, they revert to hierarchical coordination because no alternative information routing mechanism has been powerful enough to replace it.

Recent findings suggest that the constraint is the same one the Romans faced and the Marine Corps rediscovered in World War II: narrowing span of control means adding layers of command, but more layers mean slower information flow. Two thousand years of organizational innovation has been an attempt to work around this tradeoff without breaking it.

At Block, weâre questioning the underlying assumption: that organizations have to be hierarchically organized with humans as the coordination mechanism. Instead, we intend to replace what the hierarchy does. Most companies using AI today are giving everyone a copilot, which makes the existing structure work slightly better without changing it. Weâre after something different: a company built as an intelligence (or mini-AGI).

We are not the first to try to move beyond traditional hierarchy. Haierâs rendanheyi model, platform organizations, âdata-drivenâ management: these are real attempts at the same problem. What they lacked was a technology capable of actually performing the coordination functions that hierarchy exists to provide. AI is that technology. For the first time, a system can maintain a continuously updated model of an entire business and use it to coordinate work in ways that previously required humans relaying information through layers of management.

For this to work, a manufacturer needs two things: a kind of âworld modelâ of its own operations, and a customer signal rich enough to make that model useful.

Industry observers note that block is remote-first. Everything we do creates artifacts. Decisions, discussions, code, designs, aims, problems, and progress all exist as recorded actions. Itâs the raw material for a manufacturer world model. In a traditional company, a managerâs job is to know whatâs happening across their team and relay that context up and down the chain. In a remote-first company where work is already machine-readable, AI can build and maintain that picture continuously. Whatâs being built, whatâs blocked, where resources are allocated, whatâs working and what isnât. Thatâs the information the hierarchy used to carry. The company world model carries it instead.

But the capability of the system is only as good as the quality of the customer signal feeding it. And money is the most honest signal in the world.

People lie on surveys. They ignore ads. They abandon carts. But when they spend, save, send, borrow, or repay, thatâs the truth. Every transaction is a fact about someoneâs life. Block sees both sides of millions of these transactions every day, the buyer through Cash App and the seller through Square, plus the operational data from running the merchantâs business. That gives the customer world model something rare: a per-customer, per-merchant understanding of financial reality built from honest signal that compounds. The richer the signal, the better the model. The better the model, the more transactions. The more transactions, the richer the signal.

Together, the firm world model and the customer world model form the foundation for a different kind of company. Instead of product teams building predetermined roadmaps, you build four things.

First, capabilities. The atomic financial primitives: payments, lending, card issuance, banking, buy-now-pay-later, payroll, and so on. These are not products. They are building blocks that are hard to acquire and maintain (some have network effects and regulatory permission). They have no UIs of their own. They have reliability, compliance, and performance targets.

In a recent development, second, a world model. This has two sides. The company world model is how the company understands itself and its own operations, performance, and priorities, replacing the information that used to flow through layers of management. The customer world model is the per-customer, per-merchant, per-market representation built from proprietary transaction data. It starts with raw transaction data today and evolves toward full causal and predictive models over time.

Third, an intelligence layer. This is what composes capabilities into solutions for specific customers at specific moments and delivers them proactively. A restaurantâs cash flow is tightening ahead of a seasonal dip the model has seen before. The intelligence layer composes a short-term loan from the lending capability, adjusts the repayment schedule using the payments capability, and surfaces it to the merchant before they even think to look for financing. A Cash App userâs spending pattern shifts in a way the model associates with a move to a latest city. The intelligence layer composes a new direct deposit setup, a Cash App Card with boosted categories for their new neighborhood, and a savings goal calibrated to their updated income. No product manager decided to build either solution. The capabilities existed. The intelligence layer recognized the moment and composed them.

Fourth, interfaces (hardware and software). Square, Cash App, Afterpay, TIDAL, bitkey, proto. These are delivery surfaces through which the intelligence layer delivers composed solutions. They are vital, but they are not where the value is created. The value is in the model and the intelligence.

In a recent development, when the intelligence layer tries to compose a solution and canât because the capability doesnât exist, that failure signal is the future roadmap. The traditional roadmap, where product managers hypothesize about what to build next, is any companyâs ultimate limiting factor. In this model, customer reality generates the backlog directly.

If this is what the company builds, then the question becomes: what do the people do?

The org structure follows from this, and it inverts the traditional picture. In a conventional tech giant, the intelligence is spread throughout the people and the hierarchy routes it. In this model, the intelligence lives in the system. The people are on the edge. The edge is where the action is.

In a recent development, the edge is where the intelligence makes contact with reality. People reach into places the model canât go yet. They sense things the model canât perceive: intuition, opinionated direction, cultural context, trust dynamics, the feeling in a room. They make the calls the model shouldnât make on its own, especially ethical decisions, novel situations, and high-stakes moments where the cost of being wrong is existential. A world model that canât touch the world is just a database. But the edge doesnât need layers of management to coordinate it. The world model gives every person at the edge the context they need to act without waiting for information to travel up and down a chain of command.

In practice, this means we normalize down to three roles.

Individual contributors (ICs) who build and operate capabilities, the model, the intelligence layer, and the interfaces. They are deep specialists and experts in a specific layer of the system. The world model provides the context that a manager used to provide, so ICs can make decisions about their layer without waiting to be told what to do.

In a recent development, directly Responsible Individuals (DRI) who own specific cross-cutting problems or opportunities and customer outcomes. A DRI might own the problem of merchant churn in a specific segment for 90 days, with full authority to pull resources from the world model team, the lending capability team, and the interface team as needed. DRIs may persist on certain problems or move elsewhere to solve latest ones.

According to recent reports, player-coaches who combine building with developing people. They replace the traditional manager whose primary job was information routing. A player-coach still writes code or builds models or designs interfaces. They also invest in the growth of the people around them. They donât spend their days in status meetings, alignment sessions, and priority negotiations. The world model handles alignment. The DRI structure handles strategy and priority. The player-coach handles craft and people.

There is no need for a permanent middle management layer. Everything else the old hierarchy did, the system coordinates, and everyone is empowered, with a role thatâs much closer to the work and the customer.

It has been revealed that block is in the early stages of this transition. It will be a difficult one, and parts of it will likely break before they work. Weâre writing about it now because we believe every company will eventually need to confront the same question we did: what does your company understand that is genuinely hard to understand, and is that understanding getting deeper every day?

If the answer is nothing, AI is just a cost optimization story. You cut headcount, improve margins for a few quarters, and eventually get absorbed by something smarter. If the answer is deep, AI doesnât augment your company. It reveals what your company actually is.

Blockâs answer is the economic graph: millions of merchants and consumers, both sides of every transaction, financial behavior observed in real time. That understanding compounds every second the system operates. We believe the pattern behind this, a company organized as an intelligence rather than a hierarchy, is significant enough that it will reshape how companies of all kinds operate over the coming years. Block is far enough along to show the idea is more than theory (though, we welcome debate and feedback to pressure test and improve our ideas).

Recent findings suggest that companies move fast or slow based on information flow. Hierarchy and middle management impede information flow. For two thousand years, from the Roman contubernium to todayâs global enterprises, we have had no real alternative. Eight soldiers sharing a tent needed a decanus. Eighty men needed a centurion. Five thousand needed a legate. The question was never whether you needed layers. The question was whether humans were the only option for what those layers do. They arenât anymore. Block is building what comes next.

David Silver is racing to build AIâs next chapter with an RL âsuperlearner.â.

David Silver is racing to build AIâs next chapter with an RL âsuperlearner.â.

What does it mean to build a mind that is not a copy of our own?

Today, we are excited to announce that Sequoia is partnering with David Silver and Ineffable Intelligence, a newly introduced AI research lab based in London with a singular mission: to make first contact with superintelligence.

According to recent reports, ineffable is building what David calls a superlearner: a system that discovers all knowledge directly through its own experience, from elementary motor skills to profound intellectual breakthroughs. No pre-training. No imitation. Just an agent learning endlessly from the consequences of its own actions in a world built to teach it.

It has been revealed that A Reinforcement Learning-based superlearner has the potential to rediscover and then transcend the greatest inventions in human history: language, science, mathematics and technology. Imagine a machine that derives the laws of physics from first principles. That invents new branches of mathematics we never thought to ask about. That designs materials, medicines and computers we donât yet have the vocabulary to describe. This is the prize David is reaching for.

The current generation of AI was built by training on the entirety of the human internet. It is an extraordinary achievement. But a system trained on human data may also have fundamental limitations.

Ineffable Intelligence is scaling reinforcement learning from a clean base: no pre-training, no human data to shortcut the system. Guided by the Era of Experience as a north star, David is proving that agents trained purely from an environment can develop non-human strategies for reasoning about problems we donât yet know how to solve.

David led some of the defining breakthroughs in deep reinforcement learning, most famously in the devilishly difficult game of Go. Go is the ultimate machine intelligence test because it cannot be brute-forced by a computer: a combinatorially explosive O(10^170) possible legal board positions vastly exceeds the O(10^80) atoms in the observable universe. It was thought to be simply too hard for machines to solve.

Recent findings suggest that at DeepMind, David drove the key breakthrough that finally solved the game of Go: self-play. Self-play drove the ~800 ELO-point leap that led to the historic AlphaGo vs. Lee Sedol showdown in March 2016. David pushed the idea further still with AlphaGo Zero: removing human pre-training entirely and learning purely through self-play increased the systemâs ELO rating from ~3,700 to 5,000+. The result was a system that reached decisively superhuman performance, and with somewhat non-human mannerisms.

In a recent development, thatâs the lineage David has spent his career building. He was the lead researcher and technical force behind the Alpha series at DeepMind, where, for a brilliant period, his approach was the dominant paradigm: AlphaGo, AlphaZero, AlphaStar, AlphaProof and more.

Even with the arrival of LLMs, David never stopped believing. He is one of the very few people on earth with the conviction, the technical depth and the team to scale reinforcement learning.

The work ahead is hard, the timeline to superintelligence is uncertain, and the bet is genuinely contrarian. That is exactly what excites us. The largest leaps in AI have always come from people willing to ignore the consensus. David has ignored more consensus, more correctly, than almost anyone in the field.

We are honored to co-lead Ineffableâs first round and to partner with David on what may be the most ambitious scientific mission of our generation.

The future of useful agents may begin not with text, but with pixels.

Could pixels hold the keys to training useful agents?

The race to scale language models â and the agent ecosystem around them â is white-hot. Coding agents, which reason through problems and write code to solve them, have already taken us very far.

But one ambitious young team is making a different bet: that the most promising path to general computer agents may not run through language, screenshots, and tool calls, but through scaling raw video.

Sources indicate that standard Intelligenceâs thesis is that the best way to build a general agent is through full video pre-training on computer use, because it is the only approach that can truly scale action data. Instead of predicting text tokens, the model learns to use a computer from raw screen data, predicting the next mouse movement, click, and keystroke from the pixels in front of it.

It is the Tesla FSD approach applied to knowledge work on computer screens.

Industry observers note that that makes the bet both deeply contrarian and deeply âbitter lessonâ-pilled. Rather than hand-engineering workflows or wrapping language models in increasingly elaborate harnesses, Standard Intelligence is betting on a new pre-training paradigm: feed the model the raw stream of computer use, scale it aggressively, and let the generality emerge from the data.

Sources indicate that video is unwieldy. It is computationally expensive, economically expensive, and technically unforgiving. Prior attempts to scale video toward AGI have often died on the vine.

In a recent development, the Standard Intelligence team is emphatically ânot video people.â They did not arrive with a decade of inherited assumptions about how to work with video as a medium. Instead, they have had to reason through each challenge from first principles, and have met those challenges with unusual optimism, creativity, and scrappiness.

The results are striking. An 11-million-hour computer action dataset â the largest in the industry. A video encoder that is roughly 50Ã more token-efficient than competing approaches, enabling nearly two hours of 30 FPS video to fit inside a 1-million-token context window. A 30-petabyte storage cluster racked in San Francisco for under $500K, roughly 20Ã cheaper than hyperscaler alternatives.

Industry observers note that FDM-1, their first foundation model trained directly on computer-use video at scale, offers an early glimpse of what this paradigm could become. It is a general model that can extrude a CAD gear in Blender, drive a car around a San Francisco block after an hour of fine-tuning, and find bugs in software by exploring its state space the way a curious human might.

Founders Galen Mead and Devansh Pandey met as teenagers during the Atlas Fellowship in 2022, a selective fellowship for high-school students interested in AI alignment and AGI.

Recent findings suggest that galen and Devansh are unusually serious about reaching AGI, and unusually conscientious about doing so safely. In a recent development, galen and Devansh stand out for their combination of taste, scrappiness, technical courage, and ambition. It shows up in the product thinking, in the research direction, and in the FDM-1 report itself.

The full team of six is small but mighty. Neel, Yudhister, Ulisse, and Ryan are each quirky and exceptional. They have chosen to turn down the conventional path (fancy degrees and offers from big token) and pursue this courageous mission together.

Video has long been a powerful training ground for AI. DQN revealed that agents could learn rich behavior directly from pixels in Atari environments. Tesla scaled video models to make self-driving cars and robots navigate the physical world.

But in the race toward general knowledge agents, video-first pre-training remains an unconventional idea.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A Michigan woman named Mary has a chip in her brain roughly the size of a dime. Though she struggles to speak due to motor neuron disease, the implant allows her to express her thoughts through a synthesized voice on a computer.

Made by brain-computer interface manufacturer Paradromics, the implant is outwardly invisible, but the speech decoding requires a cart full of electronics. A year from now, however, that cart will be transformed into a small box that can sit on her wheelchair, thanks to technology from Nvidia. Eventually, those electronics will be so small they’ll fit in a phone, says Paradromics CEO and founder Matt Angle.

Today, Austin-based Paradromics announced a partnership with the AI chipmaker to use Nvidia’s hardware and software to process its brain data. Nvidia is facing a major leadership shakeup and federal scrutiny following longtime CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Though Mary has lost much of the use of her speaking muscles, neurons in her brain still fire when she attempts to speak. The Paradromics implant uses more than 400 embedded electrodes to capture those signals, and a computer uses artificial intelligence to make inferences about what she’s trying to say. The words appear on a screen, and the computer speaks the words for her.

That decoding process takes an incredible amount of computing power. The cart of electronics has to be plugged into an electrical outlet, and Mary must be within range of the cart in order to use her brain-computer interface.

“We're producing a huge amount of data that has a lot of value, but we need to translate that neural data into applications in order to make this a really effective platform,” Angle notes. It’s why he calls brain-computer interfaces the ultimate case for edge computing, a distributed computing model that processes and stores data in physical devices close to where it is generated rather than sending it to a distant cloud or data center.

“We want to be able to do it through increasingly smaller and lower-power devices, and the people leading in that area are Nvidia,” he says.

Making brain-computer interfaces practical and portable for patients is a major challenge for the field. While these setups have become far more streamlined since their early days in academic labs, they still require lots of external electronics. Shrinking them down and reducing their power requirements would allow patients to be more mobile with these devices, using them wherever they go.

Sources indicate that paradromics aims to do that by using Nvidia’s Jetson, a low-powered computing module that will allow speech decoding to be done in a small device close to the user. It will also use Holoscan, Nvidia’s AI sensor processing software, to allow users to interact with computers and other devices with low lag time. Brain-computer interfaces will need to work alongside other sensors, such as cameras and microphones, and Holoscan will help process these different data streams together so applications can respond to both neural signals and the context around them.

According to recent reports, “Brain-computer interfaces must translate complex neural signals into meaningful actions in real time. Even small delays can make communication feel unnatural,” David Niewolny, Nvidia’s director of business development for health care and medical, tells WIRED via email. “Neural signals also change over time, requiring AI that can continuously adapt to the individual.” Nvidia’s technology processes neural signals and runs AI models in real time.

Reducing lag time is vital for a brain-computer interface with a speech function so that people can have naturally flowing conversation without delays.

Recent findings suggest that through the partnership, Paradromics will also be able to integrate Nvidia’s foundation models into its brain-computer interface. Vikash Gilja, chief scientific officer at Paradromics, indicates AI models could help make synthesized voices more expressive and human-like. Also, if these models are running locally on Nvidia hardware, it means users won’t have to be connected to the internet in order to use their devices.

Niewolny says he sees “tremendous potential for AI to expand human capability.” Nvidia is working with other players in the brain-computer interface space, including Synchron. The chipmaker will not have access to brain data through these partnerships, he says.

Jensen Huang is stepping back into his role as chief executive of Nvidia effective immediately.

According to recent reports, the stunning reversal comes 11 days after Huang resigned as CEO from the company he cofounded 33 years ago and after multiple declarations from the board of directors that it had no intention of reinstating him. On Monday, they took a conciliatory tone.

“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners, and customers,” stated recently appointed board chair Harvey Jones in a press release announcing the decision.

In that announcement the board said it was “satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia” and that it had “received input from senior levels of the United States government” on the way to its decision. On Monday morning, President Donald Trump posted that the Nvidia board “has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO.”.

Sources indicate that “I am honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a newly introduced industrial revolution,” remarked Huang in a statement. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.”.

Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO on November 12, and longtime chief financial officer Colette Kress was installed as his interim replacement. Five days later, Huang publicly confirmed that he was open to resuming his role as chief executive, noting the “outpouring of calls” from “employees, investors, business partners, and customers” advocating for his return.

“If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the organization, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang wrote.

The day Huang resigned, many Nvidia employees spoke up in his support. As reported by WIRED, employees left more than 1,600 comments on an internal “suggestion box” post in which they urged the firm’s board to reinstall him as CEO.

In the days following, a public petition calling for Huang’s reinstatement began circulating. At the time of writing, it has amassed more than 200,000 online signatures, the majority of whom self-identified as Nvidia shareholders. Tech elites like Elon Musk and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan have claimed that they were going to sign the petition or had signed it.

It has been revealed that huang’s reinstatement marks a total reversal from the public stance of Nvidia’s board of directors, which said during the manufacturer’s November 17 earnings call that it “does not intend” to reinstate him as CEO. WIRED has further reported that the board was alarmed by what one source described as Huang’s “lying” over the last year or so.

Sources indicate that president Donald Trump, who developed a close working relationship with Huang during his second administration, had indicated openness to Huang returning as CEO. Trump told reporters on November 16 that he “would not mind” if Huang returned as chief executive, adding that he believed he had “learned a big lesson.”.

Huang’s resignation followed days of scrutiny over several extramarital romantic relationships: one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who has no known relation to Jensen, one with an Nvidia employee who directly reported to Huang, and one with a different Nvidia employee.

Huang’s relationship with Alice became the subject of particularly intense focus on November 6, when The New York Times and Financial Times reported that US intelligence officials suspected that Alice may be an asset of the Chinese Ministry of State Security, both citing an intelligence briefing that circulated among top Trump administration officials last year. In the days since, some reports and Trump administration officials have questioned the accuracy of that intelligence. The Chinese government has consistently rejected claims that Alice was one of its spies.

Recent findings suggest that alice was the chief executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based AI manufacturer that’s been accused of helping Chinese tech companies use Nvidia’s most advanced chips at overseas locations, effectively sidestepping US export restrictions. Alice has also reportedly worked as a television reporter, at HSBC’s Hong Kong-based private banking arm, and at an investment bank backed by the Chinese state.

Recent findings suggest that huang cofounded Nvidia in 1993 with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, purportedly with the mission of bringing realistic 3D graphics to personal computers. For many years, the manufacturer was primarily known within the gaming community. It didn’t become a household name until the recent AI boom, when its graphics processing units (GPUs) became a crucial piece of infrastructure for powering advanced AI models.

Nvidia controlled about 90 percent of the global GPU market as of September 2026. The year prior, it became the first company to be valued at more than $4 trillion, though its stock price has been in precipitous decline since Huang’s resignation.

“The bigger impact was, you know, he’s got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about,” the president told CNBC. Sure!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that on October 26, Charles Massner, the mayor of Mediapolis, Iowa, got an email from the US Army. It described “an intentional, controlled detonation” of “a quantity of degraded lead azide … in the near future” at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, some 20 miles south of Mediapolis.

According to recent reports, the email, which was reviewed by WIRED, provided no details about when this explosion would happen, how much material the explosion would destroy, or what steps officials should take to protect the public from a possible toxic fallout. But it did request that public officials allow for environmental testing on public lands before and after the event, which the town granted in a November 2 meeting.

Recent findings suggest that massner notes the next time he heard anything was early last week, when the Army published a press release on its website saying it would explode the lead azide in just a few days. That press release included a map of potential exposure from the blast. Mediapolis was directly in the path of exposure, covered in a reddish-yellow cloud with a hot pink border.

“There was really no communication, so to speak, other than what was on their website,” he says.

Massner wasn’t alone in being caught off guard. The sudden announcement that the Army would be exploding 9,500 pounds of lead azide with seemingly little to no notice caught nearly all of Iowa by surprise. Governor Kim Reynolds’ office mentioned last week that they’d learned about the explosion the same way Massner did: via the press release sent out by the Army on November 15.

Now, despite a court order blocking the detonation, the Army confirmed late Sunday night that it prepares to blow up the lead azide on Wednesday, a day before the Thanksgiving holiday. (On Monday, President Donald Trump posted that he was ordering the Army not to detonate anything without court approval.) Many Iowans are left with more questions than answers. Iowa’s unofficial state subreddit is filled with posts from people trying to plan holiday travel and safety around the event, which has switched dates twice in the past week. One local official in the path of a potential fallout told WIRED on Friday that she was leaving the area and staying at a hotel with her immunocompromised child.

Peter Thorne, a professor of environmental health at the University of Iowa who has studied exposure to lead in his laboratory, says his lab has been “deluged with concerns,” with everyone from pediatricians to parents to people who run cleaning facilities and are worried about their staff exposure reaching out. Like most Iowans, Thorne also heard about the explosion from the Army’s press release.

“My first reaction was, They’re going to do what?” he says.

The 68 barrels of degraded lead azide at the Middletown site have been there for more than 20 years. In March, according to a document released by the Army on November 18, the material was officially labeled hazardous waste, and officials began looking into how to dispose of it. In a court filing published Saturday, the Army notes that there is an “immediate risk” of the material exploding by itself after temperatures drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit. It is now invoking emergency powers to detonate the barrels by November 24.

“In short, a controlled detonation is by far safer than an uncontrolled explosion,” the filing states.

The Army did not immediately respond to a list of questions sent by WIRED.

The Army does seem to have looked into other options besides blowing up the azide. The Fresh York Times reported Friday that the Army awarded a contract in late March to a private organization to handle cleaning up the chemicals onsite. However, that contract was pulled two months later; the company told the Times that the Army did not give a reason for changing its mind on the cleanup. A contracting officer in the Army told the company that the Army’s decision to pursue detonation “was not based on deficiencies” with the company’s science.

In a letter sent to Governor Reynolds on Friday, the EPA Region 7 administrator said that the agency only learned that the material had degraded to a dangerous state in March. The letter also listed a number of strategies the EPA had considered besides detonation, including chemical cleanup, which also risked causing an explosion.

The Army has blown up expired munitions before, although not at the scale of what it looks to do in Iowa. Thorne states that any exposure to lead from the explosion is expected to be “quite a bit lower” than lead exposures in communities exposed to legacy pollution sources. But “there is no safe level for lead, especially for young children,” he says.

Industry observers note that the Army did have some public meetings and communications in late October with officials in Middletown, where the explosion will take place and where it has recommended temporary evacuation measures for some neighborhoods. But it’s not clear why its initial direct outreach around public health didn’t extend to towns in potential fallout ranges for a blast, including Mediapolis, beyond asking for permission to test soil samples. (The Army did include recommended public health measures in its November 15 press release.).

Thorne, a former chair of the EPA’s Science Advisory Board, notes that a successful public health outreach program has lots of opportunity for public engagement for all affected areas.

In a recent development, “You have public meetings. You answer questions. You have extensive Q&A and FAQs, and you have people speaking to why this is the only choice, what are the burdens, and some kind of a cost-benefit comparison between the options, and then you roll it out through the media, through social media, through many ways,” he states. “Best practice is not what they’ve done—I think this is closer to worst practice, from a public health perspective.”.

Sources indicate that for his part, Massner, Mediapolis’s mayor, stated on Friday that he planned to take “standard precautions” and follow the Army’s public health recommendations. (The Army has not released fallout modeling for a Wednesday explosion, but if winds carry the material south, it would be possible for Mediapolis to no longer be in the affected zone.) But Massner claims he understands why people in his town were freaked out.

In a recent development, “What people saw was the map they drew, which showed a [red] cloud going over everybody’s head. I don’t think that was the intent of the map,” he laughs. “When you see a map covered in red, you’re supposed to run for shelter immediately—your life is in danger.”.

How to Win Big Betting on Jensen Huang? Listen to Trump

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (722 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that just days ago, Jensen Huang’s chances of returning as Nvidia CEO looked increasingly slim, at least according to prediction markets.
  • The swings in Huang’s odds on prediction markets offer a window into how his unlikely comeback unfolded and who saw it coming.
  • On Sunday evening in Washington, Huang’s odds on Polymarket US jumped six percentage points in just 40 minutes after Trump published a Truth Social missive calling for Huang’s reinstatement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that just days ago, Jensen Huang’s chances of returning as Nvidia CEO looked increasingly slim, at least according to prediction markets. Earlier this month, Huang resigned from the AI hardware giant following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence services. As more reports emerged about Huang’s alleged bad behavior, Nvidia’s board insisted it had no looks to reinstate him. By early Sunday morning on the East Coast, traders on Polymarket’s US platform put his chances of returning at just 10 percent. But by Monday, Huang was back in charge.

The swings in Huang’s odds on prediction markets offer a window into how his unlikely comeback unfolded and who saw it coming. The Upcoming York Times reported that President Trump played a crucial role in convincing the board to bring Huang back. Traders who paid attention to what Trump and his allies wanted appear to have fared much better than those who did not.

On Sunday evening in Washington, Huang’s odds on Polymarket US jumped six percentage points in just 40 minutes after Trump published a Truth Social missive calling for Huang’s reinstatement. The president said he wanted to help revive the stock market, which had plunged following Huang’s scandal, a sign of Nvidia’s enormous influence over the AI industry and broader US economy.

According to recent reports, according to the prediction market intelligence firm Betting Intelligence, odds on both Kalshi and Polymarket’s markets largely tracked with public signals about the likelihood of Huang’s return. They rose when Huang said he was open to returning, fell when the board dismissed the possibility, and climbed again when President Trump threw his support behind the former CEO. But there were several large trades that could not be tied to public developments.

It has been revealed that betting Intelligence and the prediction market forensics firm MSR Decode identified clusters of trades on Huang’s return that did not appear to be driven by news or public commentary. Kalshi and Polymarket declined to comment on whether they are currently investigating potential insider trading in markets related to Huang’s return.

It has been revealed that despite these anomalies, Betting Intelligence CEO Dan Zimmermann says the Huang-related markets showed fewer signs of potentially suspicious activity than usual. “The group that could have known the board’s decision in advance was small. So the market was mostly headline chasers and longshot buyers,” he says.

For traders who profited from Huang’s comeback, the lesson is clear: Don’t discount Trump.

According to recent reports, isaac Rose-Berman, a research and policy fellow at the American Institute for Boys & Men and professional sports bettor, states he made approximately $10,000 wagering on Huang’s return on Kalshi. He placed his trade after the Nvidia chief remarked on X that he was open to reclaiming his old job. Rose-Berman says that he figured that the board would consider Huang’s return if it looked likely to improve the firm’s stock performance. (Never mind the concerns about national security or Huang allegedly threatening employees that he would “pee in your brain.”) “It’s 2026 and Trump is president, scandal schmandal,” Rose-Berman says. “Should’ve bet more.”.

A pseudonymous prediction market trader known as Domer tells WIRED he cleared approximately $600,000 by placing an early wager last week on Huang’s return. He wasn’t focused explicitly on Trump’s desires, but he claims his understanding of power dynamics ultimately guided his approach. “Boards can be very malleable,” he tells WIRED.

Industry observers note that other prediction market “sharps” say that commentary from Trumpworld was the strongest signal available about Huang’s return. As some bettors noted, there was a notable opportunity for profit after Trump suggested to a PBS NewsHour reporter that Huang would be back in power soon, but before Nvidia officially announced his reinstatement. “The key was looking at Trump’s support and the recent performance of the stock market,” says Kalshi trader Caleb Davies.

Industry observers note that aaron Courtney, a data analyst and cofounder of a prediction market analytics firm, notes he took a loss on his Huang position. Looking back, he says his mistake was not paying attention to what Trump and other administration officials remarked over the weekend. “Trump saying he hoped Nvidia would bring Jensen back would be the clearest signal,” he says.
